item.title: Promotions Gallery in Paris, France
item.description:
Historically, a secret entrance at the School of Mines, known as the “Mines staircase,” provided students access to the Paris Catacombs.

Although this private access is no longer available for use due to safety reasons, the General Inspector of Quarries still grants students permission to uphold this artistic tradition.

Each year, on the occasion of Sainte-Barbe, celebrated on December 4th in honor of the patron saint of miners, first-year students create a painting representing their class, continuing the tradition.

item.title: Čigoč Stork Village in Kratečko, Croatia
item.description:
In the Croatian village of Čigoč, some of the most conspicuous residents live above the rooftops. White storks build bulky nests on traditional wooden houses, sharing the settlement with the people below.

Situated in Lonjsko Polje Nature Park beside the Tišina oxbow of the Sava River, the village is surrounded by wet meadows, pastures, and pools. These habitats provide feeding grounds close to the nests, allowing adult birds to gather frogs, insects, and other small animals for their young.

In 1994, the conservation foundation EuroNatur named Čigoč the first European Stork Village. The designation recognised the village’s importance for white storks and its long-standing relationship between people, traditional farming, and wildlife. It also launched an initiative that would connect stork villages across Europe.

The wooden houses are part of this story. Their rooftops provide nesting places, while the surrounding agricultural landscape helps sustain the birds. During the breeding season, a walk through the village offers a chance to watch adults tending their nests and travelling between the rooftops and nearby feeding grounds.

item.title: Thunder Hole in Bar Harbor, Maine
item.description:
Located in Maine's Acadia National Park, along the rocky shoreline of Mount Desert Island, Thunder Hole is a natural geological formation known for producing a  booming, thunder-like sound phenomenon that gives it its name, as well as for explosive water sprays reaching up to 40 feet.

Resulting from glacial activity over thousands of years ago, what began as a small, natural fissure in the solid granite cliffs, slowly gave way to the 10 foot wide channel seen today. As high tide rolls in, and wave force increases, water rushes into this channel, and into a small underwater cavern contained therein.

When an incoming wave forces water into this cavern, trapped air in the cavern is compressed and then escapes, almost as if through the blow hole of a whale, with magnificent water sprays and reverberating claps that sound like thunder. 

Stand in awe on this rocky outcropping, as you take in the sweeping coastal views and the natural wonders that Mother Nature has provided. 

Thunder Hole is best viewed approx 2 hours before high tide (check google for tide tables).

item.title: Abdulla Avloni Memorial Museum in Tashkent, Uzbekistan
item.description:
Most memorial museums stay put in the house of the person they remember. This one moved out.

It was founded in 1968 in the Tashkent house where Abdulla Avloni (1878–1934) had lived with his family from 1910 until his death. Avloni was one of the Jadids, the Muslim reformers who believed Central Asia could be renewed through new-method schools, newspapers and the theatre. He opened schools, wrote their textbooks, published the newspaper Shuhrat and, in 1913, gathered the Turon theatre troupe.

In 1993 the museum left the house for the institute that carries Avloni's name, where teachers from all over Uzbekistan now come to brush up their skills. Without its original walls, it relies on things to bring him close: his desk, typewriter and candlestick, his bookcase and wardrobe, even his clothes, arranged in a reconstruction of his study.

Around them are early twentieth-century books and newspapers in Arabic script, printed in Tashkent, Kazan, Orenburg, Baku and Istanbul, and a small stage that recalls the Turon troupe. The most surprising corner is a tall red display in the middle of the hall, where Avloni and fellow reformers such as Mahmudkhoja Behbudi, brought to life with artificial intelligence, look out at visitors and present passages from their writings. Walk around to the back and there is a mirror with the words "Zamonamiz jadidi", "a Jadid of our time". Whoever looks into it becomes, for a moment, the newest member of the movement.

The museum is also the only one from Uzbekistan in the UMAC Worldwide Database of University Museums and Collections.

item.title: Podcast: Exploring Alberta’s Rich History in Fiction
item.dc:creator: The Podcast Team
item.description:
Listen and subscribe on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and all major podcast apps.

In this episode of The Atlas Obscura Podcast, we’re exploring the surprising side of Alberta with the Canadian novelist Esi Edugyan.

Our podcast is an audio guide to the world’s wondrous, awe-inspiring, strange places. In under 15 minutes, we’ll take you to an incredible site, and along the way you’ll meet some fascinating people and hear their stories. Join us daily, Monday through Thursday, to explore a new wonder with host Kelly McEvers and guests.

This is an edited transcript of the Atlas Obscura Podcast: a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. Find the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and all major podcast apps.

Esi Edugyan: I remember coming across this image of these Black homesteaders in Central and Northern Alberta kind of working the land. I hadn't had a sense of there being any Black presence or Black history in Alberta, and I thought, "Oh my gosh, who are these people?"

Kelly McEvers: I'm Kelly McEvers, and this is Atlas Obscura, a celebration of the world's strange, incredible, and wondrous places. This episode was produced in partnership with Travel Alberta: Explore Canada's Wild Side. This month we are talking to writers and artists who find inspiration in their home province of Alberta.

And today we're talking to novelist Esi Edugyan. She grew up in Calgary, Alberta, and her novels are part literary fiction, part adventure, traveling across continents and through different time periods. They're also based on her extensive historical research. She says she's inspired by what she calls the footnotes of history, these moments and stories that most of us have never heard of, in particular stories and histories of Black communities.

And today she is taking us on a tour of the places in Alberta that have shaped her life and work, from a prehistoric buffalo jump to the ghost towns of Black homesteaders. Esi Edugyan, thank you so much for being here today.

Edugyan: Delighted to be here.

McEvers: Okay, so for people who are not familiar with Calgary or Alberta, how would you describe it?

Edugyan: You know, it's, it's so funny. I realize my Alberta is like a remembered Alberta. Love that. It's like an Alberta of the imagination, simply because I haven't really lived there since 1995. For me, Alberta is like, we used to call it Big Sky country, like enormous open skies.

I think parts of it are, obviously when you get kind of outside of the cities, probably still that way. Rolling fields of wheat and farms and wonderful air. You know, I'm from Calgary. In the times that I've been returning it's very much like a city for foodies now, like excellent restaurants.

It's always had a very interesting kind of cultural landscape in terms of acts it's been able to attract, in terms of music, excellent art exhibits. So it's this kind of curious and interesting mix of, I guess, the rural and the urban. It's a very interesting place. Very interesting place.

McEvers: You grew up there in the '80s, right? What was your community like then in Calgary?

Edugyan: Definitely I was a child of the '80s, running around Calgary. I was born and raised in the southwest in a little neighborhood called Glamorgan. I grew up in a series of townhouses that were just off, like, Sarcee Trail. And as a child, I could just throw open the door, go outside, stand on my front stoop and just turn my head to the right and look out, and I could see the Rockies very clearly.

This is like one of the, the central images of my childhood is this very crisp, very pristine view of the Rocky Mountains. By the time I was a teenager, you could not see the Rocky Mountains from my stoop. But that just tells you just how quickly change happens within Calgary and the province in general, and that it came from having a very sort of austere, almost removed kind of sense of things.

Like I remember tumbleweed would be rolling through our streets as a child, and if I think of that now, that seems so weird. But yeah, we had actual like large balls of tumbleweed that would just go flowing through and you really felt that like Western ...

McEvers: And your parents came from Ghana, right?

Edugyan: Yeah. So in terms of community, like you were asking earlier, we were very much part of this web of, I guess, African immigrants and expatriates, but also just, like, a larger immigrant community. We knew people from everywhere, newcomers who would... You know, my father's, one of his best friends was this man from Poland, and then he had another best friend who was from England, and it was very interesting, a lovely kind of mix.

But, you know, I also felt myself, having been born and raised there, to just sort of be part of, I guess, this community of Canadian kids who were all kind of running around.

McEvers: So you said you left Calgary in 1995, and you now live on Vancouver Island. But thinking about Alberta and growing up there, what are some of your favorite places there?

Edugyan: I guess, my favorite places in Alberta, from when I was a child were... I think first and foremost, the things you remember are the places that you went to on, like, school field trips.

You know, I remember going to Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump. I think it's about 15 minutes from Fort Macleod, so south of Calgary. And this is a very old site, like 6,000 years old, so very, very prehistoric, where the Blackfoot would, I guess, round up the buffalo, and they would run them one route that the buffalo could take because it's going to lead them off the cliff.

And this was a very efficient way of hunting. And so right up until, I think, the mid-1800s, this was the main way that the buffalo were hunted on the plains. And now it is, I believe it's like a UNESCO World Heritage site.

It just feels like a very special place, and you know, I haven't been there since I was a child, but I can distinctly remember the feel of it, that sense of standing on the precipice of the main run and looking out onto this vast landscape of grasses and that great big sky, and just feeling this kind of, like, haunted feeling.

This is one of those memorable places that I think everybody should see.

McEvers: Yeah. Yeah, definitely. Others that sort of stick out for you?

Edugyan: Yeah, I mean, just a lot of things within Calgary itself. There's the Globe Cinema, which is one of those institutions that's been around since, like, the early to mid-'90s, where you could always go and watch, you know, art-house films.

I just remember my first experience of watching, like, a David Cronenberg film at that theater, and it just making such an impression, and attracted to, I don't know, this very kind of easily accessed art.

McEvers: Esi eventually moved to the States for graduate school at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore. Her partner was three hours away studying at the University of Virginia. And it was there in the library that she would find a historical footnote that would inspire her first novel, “The Second Life of Samuel Tyne.”

Edugyan: And I remember visiting him one weekend and just going through the stacks at the library at the University of Virginia, which is quite an incredible library. But, like, coming across a history book about Alberta, and I think when you're a kid living in Alberta, like, that's the last thing you want to pick up is a history book on Alberta.

You know, as somebody who was living away and maybe, um — not homesick, but just kind of had a thought like, “Oh, like, like I don't...” You know, we did learn some Albertan history, but I didn't feel like I had extensive knowledge or anything like that. And, uh, also, you know, you're casting around, I think with your first novel, this is not for the case for everybody, but I think with first novels, you can have the sense of wanting to kind of like stake your ground or like, “This is what I'm going to write about.”

And also you want write maybe from your experience and it's like, “Okay, I'm an Albertan, uh, so what’s in this history of Alberta?” And, I remember like by page maybe like 30 or something, coming across this image of these Black homesteaders in Central and Northern Alberta kind of working the land.

I hadn't had a sense of there being any kind of a Black presence or Black history in Alberta. And I thought, “Oh my gosh, who are these people?”

McEvers: After the break, Esi tells us who these Black homesteaders were and how they got to Northern Alberta, and how this inspired her first novel.

And we're back. I'm Kelly McEvers, your host. Esi, before the break, you talked about coming across these Black Albertan homesteaders in a history book, and you'd never heard of their story growing up. What did you find out about them?

Edugyan: So I ended up doing some research and just being completely floored to understand that there had been these small Black townships kind of scattered throughout Alberta and Saskatchewan in which freedmen, like people who'd been previously enslaved, come up from Oklahoma mainly, but also from Texas, and come and settle some of the land up north.

And why they did this, or how they ended up doing this, was because, I guess, the turn of the 20th century, the Albertan government put in place a campaign called the Last Best West, in which they were trying to encourage American farmers and ranchers to come and settle parts of the west. And so they had people actually going down, I guess, emissaries with advertisements and, like, holding talks about why this was sort of the best place for, for these people from Oklahoma and Texas.

And a lot of these freedmen thought this sounded like, you know, a great idea because since the abolition of slavery in the South, you know, they had had just the worst time trying to establish lives for themselves. They were completely disenfranchised. They were denied the vote. It was very difficult to purchase property.

There were just all sorts of restrictions in place. And so I think very slowly you had, uh, maybe it was, like, between probably about 1908 and maybe 1911, you had people coming up and kind of claiming their parcels of land. But some people did not regard these newcomers as welcome, and so there was a lot of sort of protest.

And I guess added to this, that kind of difficulty, was the fact that so much of what... For instance, if you were a farmer in Oklahoma, the crops that you would have grown were not the same crops that you would find in Alberta, so where the land is just much different. So I think it was quite difficult. And also the government, I believe, sort of dissuaded, uh, more immigration.

And so these communities were maybe capped around 1,000 people.

McEvers: At its height, Amber Valley was a thriving Black community with log cabins, a school, and fields of crops. In the book, “The Second Life of Samuel Tyne,” Esi sets the story in a fictionalized version of Amber Valley, imagining it as a still functioning community in the 1960s.

The title character, Samuel, is an immigrant from Ghana who moves his family to the crumbling buildings of the original settlement, hoping to start over and reinvent himself.

Edugyan: And, you know, they had several hundred people living there. They had kind of their own community established. They even had their own fearsome baseball team that would go and compete against other communities.

And they existed for many decades, right up until the 1950s, when their descendants decided that it would probably be easier to make a living in the cities. And so many people traveled down to Edmonton and Calgary. And so now I believe Amber Valley is like a bit of a ghost town, but you can still kind of go and, and see a few of the, the old buildings that existed.

McEvers: What is it, what was it about these settlers and their story that, you know, compelled you, that made you think, "People have to know about this," right? Like, "I need to make this into a book."

Edugyan: I think for me, the fact that I could grow up my whole life in Alberta, born and raised, and not once in any of my time there did I ever hear even the briefest sort of whiff of this history.

Like, I had no sense at all that, that these communities had existed, and I thought, "What a shame that we don't have a sense of, yeah, of this presence."

McEvers: Did you visit Amber Valley when you were doing research?

Edugyan: I did. We were visiting my father in Calgary, and then we hopped in the car and drove for several hours, uh, up to Amber Valley and just walked around some of the old buildings and saw the old baseball diamond, uh, where they used to play.

And we spoke to some of the locals in a nearby town who said... Actually, there's one man who, you know, he's ancient now, but he's been, he's sort of one of the last, I guess, settlers from that community. And they said, "You can go speak to him, but he's very grumpy, and if you ring his doorbell, he may be very unhappy."

And we didn't want to disturb him and disturb his peace, and so we kind of left it to our impressions of the landscape.

McEvers: And the main character is a immigrant from Ghana who's living in Amber Valley in a much later time. What made you wanna have this location be the backdrop to his story?

Edugyan: What I sort of felt maybe in writing “Samuel Tyne” that here was a man who felt completely, like, blindsided by the direction that his life had taken, just totally blown off course and looking for a sense of connection and community.

And so he is in some ways trying to reclaim this sense of a Black community for himself because he feels so totally divorced from his life in Calgary and any of the people in it. He feels like it's going to be a kind of a homecoming. And in the book, there's still an existing town. It's not like it was, he was returning to a ghost town only to do this.

McEvers: So your other novels, “Washington Black” and “Half-Blood Blues,” take place outside of Alberta, and I was wondering, do you see a connection between the journeys of the characters that you've created and these real-life settlers of Amber Valley?

Edugyan: I think maybe the thing that connects all of those stories is this idea of a character, usually a character from the African diaspora, searching for a sense of place or a sense of home like, looking to see themselves within the setting or the landscape that they're in.

Like, looking for some sense of continuity or looking to locate themselves within a history, but also looking to see if that history isn't there, to see how it is that they can create their own sense of home.

McEvers: Yeah. I love that throughline. You also wrote a collection of essays called “Out of the Sun,” where you talk about Blackness and identity and how that's been represented in art and culture.

And one thing you discuss are ghost stories in Canada. Why do you think ghost stories are an important part of understanding a place?

Edugyan: Yeah, I feel like ghost stories are kind of like the cult history of a place, so like the pop culture history. You know, they're not just like the lore of a place, but they're actually telling us in a way that they're, first of all, conceived, and second of all, how they kind of change throughout, you know, in the telling, throughout various decades, you know, various years.

They're expressing, I think, certain anxieties that existed in the culture at that time. You know, they're really reflective of what it is that's sort of most concerned us.

McEvers: Ah yes. Of course. What are we afraid of?

Edugyan: Yeah, what are we afraid of?

McEvers: What we're afraid of tells us so much about who we are, doesn't it?

Edugyan: Exactly. I sort of do argue that what we're afraid of, I think, really, um, really a reflection of what it is we value now. And it's always constantly changing. It's like, like a secret history of place.

McEvers: Yeah. I would love to talk about one example. One story you talk about is a friend's experience on a farm in Northern Alberta. Like, what made you think that was a ghost story that could kinda connect us?

Edugyan: Yeah, so that was, um, I had a friend whose, I don't know if his parents are still living there.

This kind of wonderfully strange, really large tract of land in Northern Alberta. They bought this home kind of on a nearby farm, and every time they left for, like, a long period of time, they'd come back and something would have happened. They returned to find their furniture being shifted a little bit.

And so I think his parents were able to kind of explain so many of these things away until it got to the point where they'd return and the light bulbs have all been taken out of the lights and piled in the center of the rug.

You know, his mother was was convinced that this was a haunting, and so she started really becoming obsessed with, who were some of the peoples who had been on that land before her. She did, of course, touch upon indigenous histories, but she didn't go too thoroughly into them to find out exactly what the stories of those particular people, you know, might be that would've created the circumstances for a haunting.

And I also thought it was interesting that this, this homestead was very close to the townships of places like Amber Valley. And, you know, she didn't really sort of look at those either. So I thought that was very interesting, the way that when we sort of look back into history, we're, we're looking for sometimes those who are are like us.

McEvers: In the essay collection "Out of the Sun,” you write that, “Slavery is not one of the ghost stories of our nations, but it should be. Its history does not haunt us, even though today I'd argue the average Canadian knows persistently little about it.”

It's almost like you're saying it should haunt us. What are the consequences when we don't listen to the ghosts, when the ghost stories are silenced?

Edugyan: Well, I think just very generally speaking, we don't have the fullest sense of our collective history, that we're sort of seeing maybe a third of the picture here.

I think that there are so many viewpoints and frames of reference for looking at, at what we would think of as a known history that even that, like, it's just so contentious.

But to look at the entire fabric, like, so to look at indigenous histories, to look at Black histories, to look at, uh, histories of Asian settlers. Like, just to look at the whole picture is to know ourselves, you know, in the fullest, uh, way possible and to have a full sense of who we are as, as a nation.

McEvers: Thank you so much for being one of the people who is bringing those stories to us. Thanks so much for being here today. We really, really, really appreciate it very much.

Edugyan: No, thank you. It's been lovely.

item.title: Binh Lam Champa Tower in Tuy Phước Đông, Vietnam
item.description:
Unlike most surviving Cham towers that crown dramatic hilltops, Binh Lam Tower rises almost unexpectedly from the flat, verdant plains of a quiet lowland village.

Constructed around the late tenth to early eleventh century, this 20-meter brick sanctuary serves as a vital architectural bridge, catching the art form mid-evolution between the delicate, lyrical features of the My Son A1 style and the grand, spear-like forms of classic Binh Dinh towers.

Its weathered facade features slender vertical pilasters, mini-temple false doors, and faint relief carvings of the mythical bird-god Garuda. Beyond its standing brickwork, Binh Lam hides deep subterranean secrets: archaeological digs uncovered vast foundations of a once-extensive religious complex, alongside stone Nagas and relief sculptures.

Furthermore, the tower once formed the eastern heart of ancient Thi Nai Citadel, positioned along river channels leading to the historical port—making this lowland monument a crucial physical anchor to Champa's lost naval and architectural empire.

item.title: National Underground Railroad Freedom Center in Cincinnati, Ohio
item.description:
The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center, located in Cincinnati along the banks of the Ohio River makes a solemn statement about the lives that were lived enslaved in the early history of the United States, and the many heroic men and women who played important roles in the Underground Railroad movement, which helped to bring an end to African slavery in the United States.  Referred to as a "museum of conscience", The Freedom Center is dedicated to exploring the struggle to abolish human enslavement. During the era when the Underground Railroad was active, Cincinnati was a major gateway across the Ohio River where freedom seekers escaped from southern slave states to the northern states or Canada, making the Center's location rather significant. 

Having opened its doors in 2004, the Freedom Center uses immersive exhibits across multiple floors to convey an account that is simultaneously rich in the cultural traditions of the enslaved, as well as steeped in the violence and tragedies that were endured.  The histories are told through a combination of permanent and traveling exhibits that utilize storytelling, film, artwork, hands-on activities and more.  

Perhaps one of the most impressive and prominent displays at the center is an authentic, 19th-century reconstructed slave pen that was obtained from a farm in Kentucky. It stands as America's only remaining, pristinely preserved slave pen and stands as a stark reminder of the atrocious conditions that were endured.

The pen, originally built somewhere around 1830 by a wealthy Kentucky farmer, runaway slave catcher, and slave trader, was used as a holding facility for captured and purchased enslaved men, women and children. It was discovered, quite by accident in 1998 when a farmer, who was preparing to demolish an old barn on his property, discovered that the barn had been built up around this old pen, thus protecting and preserving (and hiding) the slave pen for more than 100 years.

During its unfortunate years of use, enslaved people would be kept in the pen, often for months, until the slave trader accumulated a large enough "stock" to march them further south to be sold. These forced marches would often cover upwards of 750 miles. Conditions in these pens would be brutal, offering no sanitation, lighting or warmth.  As many as 65 enslaved people would often be housed in this small pen.  Also very moving is the memorial room dedicated to the Transatlantic Slave Trade, as well as the Freedom's Eternal Flame Terrace which overlooks the Ohio River and the city skyline. 

The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center is a beautiful and meaningful tribute to the human right for freedom, and to the brave men, women and children who stood up to the inhuman treatment of themselves and of others; and to those who continue to fight for the cause of freedom through out the world today.

item.title: Veliki Kalnik Castle in Koprivnica, Croatia
item.description:
Above the village of Kalnik in northern Croatia, the walls of Veliki Kalnik Castle rise from a jagged rocky ridge. Built across several levels, the medieval stronghold follows the natural contours of the rock, making its surviving towers and walls appear to grow out of the mountain.

First documented in 1243, the castle is best known for a story involving King Béla IV of Hungary and Croatia. According to local legend, the king took refuge here during the Mongol invasion of the 13th century. As the siege dragged on and supplies dwindled, villagers kept the defenders fed with plums.

The grateful king is said to have rewarded his rescuers with noble status. They became known as the kalnički šljivari—the “plum nobles of Kalnik.” This tale remains part of the region’s identity, connecting an imposing fortress with an unexpectedly humble fruit.

The ruins visible today developed over centuries. Their towers, fragments of walls, and elevated viewpoints reveal how the builders used the steep terrain as part of the castle’s defenses. From the heights, the view opens across the villages, fields, and wooded hills below.

item.title: The Crucified Tongkonan of Tolu Deri in North Toraja Regency, Indonesia
item.description:
In the highland villages of North Toraja, the skyline is dominated by tongkonan—traditional ancestral houses with sweeping, boat-shaped saddle roofs that loom dramatically over the landscape. For centuries, these wooden structures have served as the spiritual and social anchor for Torajan clans, decorated strictly according to Aluk Todolo ("the way of the ancestors"), the indigenous animist belief system. Their facades are traditionally adorned with carved geometric patterns (pa'ssura'), water buffalo horns (kabongo'), and sculpted wooden heads (katik) symbolizing wealth, status, and protection.

However, in the small hamlet of Tolu Deri, just north of Rantepao, one particular tongkonan stands out as a striking, visually arresting symbol of modern Torajan syncretism. Mounted directly onto the front gabled peak of the structure—occupying the exact position traditionally reserved for ancestral motifs—is a massive wooden crucifix bearing a carved figure of Jesus Christ.

While the majority of the Torajan population converted to Christianity (predominantly Dutch Reformed Protestantism and Catholicism) during the 20th century, the integration of Christian motifs into traditional architecture usually remains subtle, such as small carved crosses on support beams or church roofs built in the tongkonan shape. Seeing a full-scale, dramatic crucifix physically fused into the facade of a traditional house—standing directly above the customary buffalo head and skull mountings—is exceptionally rare.

This unique blending of iconographies visually captures the lived reality of Toraja today: a culture where deeply rooted Christian faith does not replace ancestral traditions, but rather sits alongside them in a harmonious, visually striking synthesis.

item.title: Negro Leagues Baseball Museum in Kansas City, Missouri
item.description:
This privately funded, not-for-profit museum lets visitors witness the greatness and trials of the teams that made up the "Original Eight" of the Negro Leagues.

 In a self guided tour explore the informative and interactive exhibits featuring the photos, artifacts and films that tell the stories of these baseball players and all the people that made these teams possible. 

Notable highlights include: 

The Exhibition Gallery Film entitled "They Were All Stars" with narration by the acclaimed James Earl Jones. This film is a museum exclusive.

A timeline of baseball and African American history along with one-of-a-kind photographs, artifacts and stories to better envision the legacies told!

The Field of Legends that allows you to step into history with a stunning recreation of a baseball diamond, featuring bronze statues of all the greatest League players in their starring positions.

item.title: Thermes Romains de Cimiez in Nice, France
item.description:
The Roman baths of Cimiez originally belonged to the ancient Roman city of Cemenelum, located in the modern district of Cimiez, Nice.

The ruins of the frigidarium of the northern baths have always been visible, never having been covered over since Roman times.  The frigidarium of the northern baths was long mistakenly called the "Temple of Apollo".

Three thermal complexes were eventually uncovered; the north, east and west complexes.  The three groups follow the same layout, with the axis and the order of the rooms are identical.

The ancient city's aqueducts brought water to the thermal complex.  The comprehensive water drainage system consists of a complex network of sewers and canals which is still visible around the site.

At the beginning of the 5th century, the first bishop of Cimiez, Saint Valerian, established the episcopal complex here made ip of a cathedral, baptistery, outbuildings, and the bishop's residence located north of the baths.  The basilica was built on the Roman walls using reused materials.  The columns from the northern baths were used in the construction of the baptistery. 

Only a tiny part of the ancient city of Cemenelum has been excavated so far.  As such there is still debate about the exact dates of the bath complexes.

item.title: Tam Thien Cave System (Tam Thiên Động) in Quy Nhon Dong, Vietnam
item.description:
Hidden along the rugged coastline near the famous Ky Co beach in Nhon Ly fishing village, Tam Thien Cave is an extraordinary system of three interconnected sea caves that remains largely unknown to most travelers.

The site is uniquely ephemeral, surfacing only for two to three months during the summer when seasonal tides and currents recede.

When the tide drops, it reveals smooth golden sandbanks inside massive stone vaults, natural rock arches, and shimmering tidal pools reflecting purple and red hues from the colorful rock walls. Visitors can explore chambers known locally as Womb Nook Cave, Purple Stone Cave, and Sky Pillar Cave via canoe or paddleboat.

Because shifting currents alter sand deposition and water levels each year, the cave system offers a completely distinct experience with every annual opening.

item.title: Astronaut Roundabout in Valdemoro, Spain
item.description:
Valdemoro, a town south of Madrid better known for its proximity to Pinto than for space exploration, has an unlikely visitor from another world standing in the middle of one of its roundabouts. Francisco Leiro’s El Astronauta, installed in 2001, has become one of the town’s most distinctive modern landmarks. The four-meter-tall stainless-steel figure appears to be taking a monumental step across the surface of the Moon—or perhaps simply trying to cross the road.

The astronaut stands on a large hemisphere designed to resemble the lunar surface. Originally conceived for the Rotonda de los Tritones, the structure was covered with dark mineral material to create the illusion of a fragment of the Moon. Today the location is known as the Glorieta del Universo, an appropriately cosmic name for a traffic circle whose principal resident has clearly travelled much farther than most of its commuters.

The sculpture is considerably more substantial than its whimsical subject might suggest. It weighs around 2,600 kilograms and was cast in stainless steel at Fundición Capa in nearby Arganda del Rey. The complicated process involved casting the work in around ten separate pieces before assembling, welding, and polishing them.

Leiro’s astronaut was intended to symbolize progress, the future, and humanity’s desire to overcome its limits. More than two decades later, it has achieved something perhaps more difficult: becoming a beloved emblem of Valdemoro. Against the otherwise empty roundabout, the gleaming figure has plenty of space to contemplate the universe—and plenty of passing drivers to contemplate him.

Will Ferguson: If you drive east from Calgary, instead of going towards Banff and the mountains, if you go the other way, the landscape will suddenly fall away and you’ll find yourself in the Badlands. But before you hit that valley, before you make that descent, if you turn off the main road, you will come to a small hidden valley full of wild roses.

In that little valley, you will find a small and improbable town—a town that should not exist. It's at the very edge of these rolling canola fields, roses, a little valley. And it certainly should not be a major theater hub by any stretch of the imagination, but it is. And Rosebud is a town that kind of defies logic.

Kelly McEvers: I’m Kelly McEvers, and this is Atlas Obscura, a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. This episode was produced in partnership with Travel Alberta. Explore Canada’s Wild Side.

This month, we're talking to writers and artists who find inspiration in their home province of Alberta. Today, we’re talking to travel writer and novelist Will Ferguson. He’s lived in South America and Japan, where he taught English for five years. But his work is inspired by his home country.

Will has published over 20 books. Many of them cover Canadian identity and history. And today, he is taking us on a tour of the province of Alberta to tell us about the places that have inspired his work. from that improbable town he was just describing, to a Japanese garden, to a town that tells the story behind a 12 foot statue of a fur trader. Will Ferguson, welcome to the show!

Will: Thanks for having me.

This is an edited transcript of the Atlas Obscura Podcast: a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. Find the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and all major podcast apps.

Kelly: For this conversation, of course, we asked you to tell us about three defining places for you in Alberta, places that have influenced your work. And before we get to those, I just want to talk a little bit about your upbringing there, if you don’t mind. Let’s just talk about growing up in Alberta. Where’s your family from? What was it like there?

Will: Well, I grew up in northern Alberta in a town, the teeming metropolis of Fort Vermilion, population 749, I believe.

Kelly: Wow.

Will: So I grew up there. That town is closer to the Arctic Circle than the American border, just by a nutshell. And I don’t know why we were proud of that. That was like a real point of pride that we were like just past the halfway point. So I always feel growing up there that I kind of emigrated to Canada. The weirdest thing is Canada, as we knew it from the radio signals and the television signals, was a southern country.

So for me, Canada was to the south. That’s how I thought of it, as a southern country with shopping malls and paved roads and traffic lights.

Kelly: Wow. That is so interesting. What an interesting way to grow up, to think of yourself from this northern land that was somehow separate from the country that you were actually in.

Will: Yes.

Kelly: I love that. When did you know you were a writer?

Will: Well, I always liked writing. I originally went to study filmmaking. I wanted to be a documentary travel filmmaker. I wanted to travel the world with these big, giant, clunky cameras people had back then. Actually, physical film. This is back in the ’80s, the late ’80s.

But I wanted to carry a tripod and a camera case and travel the world. And so I went to York University to study film production. And I learned two things at film school. One is I did not want to make films. I did not enjoy it. The second is that I like the screenwriting. I like that aspect of it, the storytelling. I always enjoyed writing. Like it was something that seemed very natural to do.

Kelly: Let’s talk about the three places you chose. Three defining places for you in Alberta. And the first one is Nikka Yuko Gardens. Tell me about that.

Will: Nikka Yuko is in southern Alberta. And southern Alberta is big sky country, is what they call it. And this is where the red-coated, you know, the mounted police, that image everyone has of the Mounties riding their horses. That’s where they first arrived. And in Southern Alberta, the reason they went there is because Southern Alberta was kind of lawless. There were these American whiskey traders coming up from Montana, causing all kinds of grief and havoc and violence among the First Nations.

So with Lethbridge, with its whiskey smuggling, Mountie police, big sky, dry plains area, it’s the last place you would ever expect to find a Zen garden, right? You never expect to find Japanese aesthetics. It’s kind of almost the opposite of what you’d expect. And there’s a history there, which I find really fascinating. That area was settled by Japanese farmers in the early 1900s. Some of them from Okinawa, which I feel so bad. I feel guilty because Okinawa is this beautiful tropical paradise where it never snows.

I don’t know who gulled them, who tricked them into coming, but they arrived in areas where the winters hit 40 below. Japanese fishermen became farmers, but they settled in there, in that area around the early 1900s.

They struggled at first, then they thrived, like it became a very Japanese area. And then in World War II, when Canada expelled Japanese citizens from the West Coast and sent them inland, often into internment camps, but not always, there was a second wave of Japanese. So there’s kind of two big waves of Japanese people in Lethbridge, in the community. So it has a long, long history and it’s still very much, there’s still very like third, fourth generation Japanese in Lethbridge. I’m only second generation Canadian. The Japanese in Lethbridge have longer roots than I have.

To commemorate this Japanese community and their history, in the 1960s, they built a beautiful Japanese garden. And I, I, want to emphasize, a real Japanese garden, like an authentic Japanese garden. They built the garden structures in Japan by master craftsmen. The tea pavilion, the bell tower, there’s wooden bridges, the cast iron Buddhist bell itself, those were brought over and assembled in Lethbridge. But the gardens themselves, like the flora, the trees, the materials, were taken from the prairies from Southern Alberta. So it’s really this perfect blend of the two.

You’ve got these Alberta skies and flora and trees and the Japanese aesthetics. So for example, they used crabapple trees for spring flowers rather than sakura. They used Canadian maples for autumn colors. They gathered stones from the Old Man River. And Nikka Yuko, it’s derived, the kanji comes from Japan-Canada friendship. Canada and Alberta is founded by so many different communities. But what I love about it is it’s such a blend of Alberta landscape and Japanese aesthetics. And my wife’s Japanese, so we go to Nikka Yuko often, whenever we can, whenever she gets homesick.

Kelly: And this place influenced your novel, Officer Shimada and the Disappearing Girl. It came out this year, in 2026. How did the place inspire the book?

Will: The population of Lethbridge has a heavy Okinawa influence. And my wife is from southern Japan, so we went down to Okinawa. And we went to this little island, the southernmost island in Japan called Hataruma, the very end of Okinawa. You can’t go any further. That’s the end of Japan. It’s maybe six kilometers across, maybe 400 people live on it. And when I was there, we walked by and there was a police station of this island with one police officer.

So I just thought, what does he do if crime comes to Hataruma? Because in front of this little tiny police station, there was a billboard with Japan’s most wanted, and these Yakuza toughs with scars on their faces. So I started to think, what is it about Okinawans that there’s something adventurous? They used to be their own kingdom. They had their own language, their own religion. They were caught between Ming China and Japan. They were their own kingdom, their own culture, but now they’re part of Japan. But they were really pulled back and forth. And I think that’s a lot of the reasons why they were open to leaving, to going across the world, to Alberta. So I believe that the roots of Okinawa’s diaspora come from being caught between two opposing empires. And Canada, of course, is in the shadow of an empire.

So I think all that stuff just kind of resonated with me and came together and came up with a novel about this officer named Shimada. on this tiny island in Okinawa who has to solve an impossible crime. So that’s kind of how it all started. It kind of starts with Nikka Yuko Gardens.

Kelly: Okay, so the next place you chose is called Rosebud. Where in Alberta is this place and what is it?

Will: Rosebud is in central Alberta. If you drive east from Calgary, Instead of going towards Banff and the mountains, if you go the other way, the landscape will suddenly fall away and you’ll find yourself in the Badlands. But just before you hit that valley, before you make that descent, if you turn off the main road, you will come to a small hidden valley full of wild roses. In that little valley, you will find a small and improbable town, a town that should not exist.

It’s at the very edge of these rolling canola fields, roses, a little valley. And it certainly should not be a major theater hub, by any stretch of the imagination, but it is. And Rosebud, is a town that kind of defies logic. So Rosebud was a prosperous little place in its day. You know, one of those classic, it was a farming and coal mining town. You know, they had homes and shops and a school, but the mine shut down, the school closed. And by the 1970s, it was a ghost town. It was essentially a ghost town. There were nine people still there, living there.

Kelly: Wow.

Will: The beauty of being almost a ghost town, the benefit of being almost empty is that there’s lots of buildings and space available. So there was a Calgary church decided to have their summer camp. And they knew someone who knew there’s all these places available in Rosebud. So they took kids out there and they had a summer camp. And among them, they also did a theater program. They put on a play for local farmers in the area. It was largely improvised. It was the ’70s, man. So it was like a theater dell’arte.

Am I saying that right? You know, like the kind of improvised 1970s style. I imagine they all had bell-bottom pants on. I could just imagine, and long hair. You know, they put on this play, and then it was such word-of-mouth spread. So it became an annual summer camp that included the arts, which included acting and theater for teens. And it grew. They grew from a summer camp to an actual theater schoo. Then it got a professional stage. And today Rosebud has a program. It runs all year. There’s three stages. One of them is outdoors. The town now has a population of about 150, but it can welcome up to 40,000 people every year.

Kelly: Wow.

Will: They have people drive out to this theater town. It’s got a beautiful bed and breakfast. There’s a hotel, a very high-end hotel. And there’s also a very cozy B&B. And there’s little antique shops. And there’s a cafe. And they’ve got some of the old town. It’s a very small little hidden valley. And my wife went to a Catholic school in Japan. And her favorite nun, the nun that she loved, was Sister Logina, who loved “Sound of Music.” So my wife grew up learning “Sound of Music.”

So we heard that they were putting on a few years ago “The Sound of Music” in Rosebud. So we drove out, stayed overnight, loved it. And what I like about Rosebud is, is you feel like you’ve discovered it. Of course you haven’t, but you feel like you’ve discovered something whenever you drive in that little valley. And it dovetails really nicely with a trip to the Badlands, to Drumheller, it’s like maybe 20 minutes away. So you can get this, it’s the contrast between these rolling canola fields that are deep green in the spring and golden yellow in the fall, and the theater. And then you drive down the hill and you're suddenly among dinosaurs and rocky hoodoo formations and fossilized remains.

That 20-25 minute drive between the two is just remarkable. And I love the fact that there’s these little communities that reinvent themselves. Because the west was always where you went to reinvent yourself. That was one of the appeals of going west. Go west, young man. Go west, young woman, west to reinvent yourself. And Rosebud kind of personifies that.

Kelly: Nice. And we should say, you feature it in your book “Meanwhile, Back in Nokomis,” which is part of your travel collection, right?

Will: Yeah, so it’s a travel collection, “Meanwhile, Back in Nokomis,” which is another small town. So it’s in there, the story of Rosebud, is in that book. And it’s a collection of the kind of, I really favor eclectic, eccentric little towns. So when you read my travel books, you’re not going to get a guide to Banff or to downtown Toronto or to Niagara Falls necessarily. But you will find out about Rosebud and Nokomis. So there you go.

Kelly: Okay, so the third place, it features in another of your travel books, “Beauty Tips from Moose Jaw.” I say place, but it’s really a statue, the 12-foot Davis statue. Talk about that.

Will: Yes. So a travel book I wrote called “Beauty Tips from Moose Jaw.” I did go to Moose Jaw. I did get beauty tips in Moose Jaw at the spa. But this is a town on the Peace River, which is a massively wide river. And the name Peace River, it sounds very calming, but it actually refers to these very bloody kind of battles between two First Nations, the Cree who pushed up and then the Beaver who fought them back.

And the Peace River became kind of the demarcation line between the two nations. So that’s where the name comes from. The gateway to northern Alberta is the town of Peace River, which is about, I think around 7,000 people. A after Peace River, you really plunge headlong into these endless forests.

But in Peace River, you will find a very iconic wooden statue of a woodsman. He’s kind of wearing what looks like a Davy Crockett-style raccoon hat. But he’s not Davy Crockett, and it’s far away from the Alamo. But it’s actually a statue of a man called 12-Foot Davis, who is real, and he was very short and stocky. Visitors sometimes think that he’s like a Paul Bunyan statue, character, that type of character. But no, he was real. He wasn’t 12 feet tall, of course.

His name was Henry Davis. And the name, how he got the name was during the Caribou Gold Rush in the 1860s up in northern Canada and BC. And he arrived too late. All the good land had been staked. But he noticed that in the rush to stake these gold claims, people were a little bit sloppy.

You’re only allowed so much space, like so many feet for a claim. And he walked through it and measured and measured, and he realized that two miners had overstaked their claim by six feet each. They’d done the math wrong, but they’d each over-claimed by six feet. So he staked a claim on 12 feet on this narrow strip of land, and he reaped a fortune in gold on those 12 feet. He made what in today would be over $200,000. So from that’s where the name 12-foot Davis, he made his fortune on this thin strip of land because he thought to check.

And he used that money and he came to the Peace River to become a fur trader. He set up his own very successful fur trading, independent fur trading fort. And he was, you know, he’s very popular in the area and friendly by all accounts.

It’s always said that he always left the door of his cabin open, which I think explains why he was robbed so often. But I’m kidding. No, he wasn’t robbed. But he did leave his cabin door open. So the idea is that if it’s windy or cold, you could always go in.

He was what’s called a free trader. So he wasn’t aligned with the big companies, the Northwest Company or the Hudson’s Bay Company. So for almost 40 years, he clashed and rankled and fought with the Hudson’s Bay Company, which wanted and claimed a monopoly on the fur trade.

So when he died, he asked to be buried. The statue is in the town, but his grave is up the hill. And he asked, and it’s a beautiful view. You get this kind of epic panorama of the Peace River and the Smoky River. It’s a very striking area. And he asked to be buried on the hill, looking down on the valley. Now, in the north, where we grew up, it was known that the reason he asked to be buried there was so that he could piss on the Hudson’s Bay Company below.

But the official reason, the official story was that you read in the tourist books is that he wanted to be buried there so that he could gaze out one last time upon the landscape that inspired and moved his heart. So again, whichever story you decide to take, it's still 12-foot Davis country. Like it belongs to the short, stocky, very astute fur trader.

Kelly: I love it. Oh, my gosh. You know, you’ve written obviously so much about Canada and about being Canadian. And, you know, you said earlier that growing up, you almost kind of grew up looking at Canada as an outsider because you lived so far north. And you obviously still live in Canada. What does it mean to you today to, you know, be Canadian?

Will: Well, what I what I like about Canada, what I enjoy the most, it’s is that it’s, do I have time? Can I tell you a very quick story about South America? Do I have time? I don’t know how podcasts work.

When I was a teenager, I went to South America with Canada World Youth. I mentioned it’s like the Peace Corps. And every Canada World Youth group was chosen to represent Canada as a whole. Like the same ratio of French to English, rural to urban, east to west.

We were like these little miniature Canadas, these groups. And they sent my group to South America. And wherever we went, the Ecuadorians would ask us to do a Canadian dance. Now we don’t have a Canadian dance. So we made one up this kind of weird square dance where we would stomp and holler and move around in circles. Um, and the Ecuadorians would be very puzzled by it.

And I’ve watched them watching this travesty of a dance we pretended was our national, and, uh, I think that in Canada, there is no homogenous attempt at a melting pot. There is no unifying Canadian culture that kind of dilutes the eclectic nature of the country. I don’t think that’s a weakness. I think that’s a strength. And I think it’s a selling point. The fact that we don’t have a Canadian dance, that it’s a very eclectic, eccentric, far-flung country. with French and English, Acadian, East, West, a wide variety.

But the key is they’re joined in this project called Canada, and there’s a civility to it. No matter what your difference is, you try your best to be civil and to be respectful. That’s it. It’s not a difficult formula. It’s not an obscure formula. It’s just we live in this very far-flung, eclectic, eccentric place. We’re only going to get along if we respect that in each other.

Kelly: Will Ferguson, thank you so much for this. This has been wonderful. You are selling me so hard on Alberta and Canada. Like, I’m in.

Will: Well, I’ll see you. I’ll be here waiting for you with a gift basket when you arrive.

Kelly: Awesome. And we’ll go to Rosebud and the Badlands and the North. All of it. Yeah. Thank you so much.

Will: Thank you.

item.description:
Our latest book, “America Obscura: An Explorer’s Guide to the Hidden Wonders of the United States,” has just been published. But it doesn’t just take you to Texas or Maine or Michigan. It takes you to a town called Hell, to a desert in one of the greenest states, to a sundial on the exact spot where America's day begins, and to a seven-story Jesus nicknamed “Our Milk Carton with Arms.”

These are real places you can visit, and they are so dang unique. Since you’ll be driving, riding the rails or flying to reach a lot of them, we built you a soundtrack to match. Every song here is tied to a specific spot in the book. The full playlist is below, but you can also stream it on Spotify.

Song Artist The place
West Coast
"White Rabbit" Jefferson Airplane Institute of Illegal Images, San Francisco: a Victorian house holding 33,000 sheets of framed LSD blotter art.
"Stash" Phish Original Stash Tribute Plaque, Estacada, Ore.: the spot in the woods where the world's first geocache, the "Stash," was hidden in 2000.
"The Goonies 'R' Good Enough" Cyndi Lauper Goonie Trails, Astoria, Ore.: Goonies never say die in the town where the movie was filmed.
"4'33\"
or "Silent All These Years"		 John Cage
or Tori Amos		 One Square Inch of Silence, Olympic National Park, Wash.: one of the quietest places in the country. Cage's piece is four and a half minutes of literal silence; Tori is the version with sound.
"Falling" Julee Cruise Twede's Cafe, North Bend, Wash.: the real Double R Diner from Twin Peaks. Order the cherry pie.
Southwest & Texas
"London Bridge Is Falling Down" Traditional London Bridge, Lake Havasu City, Ariz.: it fell all the way to Arizona, with a voodoo doll sealed inside.
"Please Mr. Postman" The Marvelettes Airmail Arrow, Reno, Nev.: before GPS, airmail pilots followed giant concrete arrows across the desert.
"Stairway to Heaven" Led Zeppelin Loretto Chapel, Santa Fe, N.M.: a "miraculous" spiral staircase built without a single nail.
"Atomic" Blondie National Museum of Nuclear Science & History, Albuquerque, N.M.: home of Atomic Annie, the cannon that fired the first and last nuclear artillery shell.
"Paris, Texas" Ry Cooder Jesus in Cowboy Boots, Paris, Texas: a cemetery statue that swapped sandals for boots.
"Cadillac Ranch" Bruce Springsteen Cadillac Ranch, Amarillo, Texas: ten Cadillacs buried nose-down in a field, and the inspiration for this song.
"Texas Sun" Khruangbin & Leon Bridges The Orange Show, Houston: a retired mail carrier's folk-art maze built from salvage, set to a Houston band.
"Bat Out of Hell" Meat Loaf Congress Bridge Bats, Austin: 1.5 million bats pour out from under the bridge on summer nights.
"My Sweet Lord" George Harrison Sri Sri Radha Krishna Temple, Spanish Fork, Utah: a Hare Krishna temple, and home to Utah's giant festival of colors.
Mountain West
"Rocky Mountain High" John Denver International Church of Cannabis, Denver: a technicolor former Lutheran church where the services are, well, elevated.
"America the Beautiful" Ray Charles Pikes Peak Summit House, Colorado: the summit that inspired the poem, now home to North America's highest donut fryer.
"Walking on the Moon" The Police Craters of the Moon, Arco, Idaho: lava fields so lunar that you can almost do the moonwalk.
"Free Fallin'" Tom Petty I.B. Perrine Bridge, Twin Falls, Idaho: the one U.S. bridge where you can BASE jump without a permit, all year.
"Tiny Bubbles" Don Ho Sip 'n Dip Lounge, Great Falls, Mont.: a tiki bar where live mermaids swim past your barstool.
"Raindrops Keep Fallin' on My Head" B.J. Thomas Hole-in-the-Wall Outlaw Hideout, Kaycee, Wyo.: where Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid hid out.
Great Plains
"Born to Lose" Ray Charles They Also Ran Gallery, Norton, Kan.: the only gallery devoted to people who lost the presidency.
"Dust in the Wind" Kansas The Big Well, Greensburg, Kan.: the largest hand-dug well in the country, in a town rebuilt after a tornado.
"On the Road Again" Willie Nelson Old Lincoln Highway, Omaha–Elkhorn, Neb.: three miles of century-old red brick on America's first coast-to-coast road.
"Chalk Dust Torture" Phish Happy Jack Chalk Mine, Scotia, Neb.: an underground chalk mine you can tour.
"Video Killed the Radio Star" The Buggles KVLY-TV Mast, Blanchard, N.D.: a 1,987-foot TV tower that was once the tallest structure on Earth.
"Oklahoma!" Rodgers & Hammerstein National Weather Museum, Norman, Okla.: storm-chasing gear in the state the musical is named for.
"A Calf Born in Winter" Khruangbin Wichita Mountains Buffalo Herd, Okla.: 650 bison descended from a Bronx Zoo breeding program.
"Time in a Bottle" Jim Croce Hall of Records, Mount Rushmore, S.D.: America's backup drive, sealed in a vault behind Lincoln's head.
Midwest
"Superman (It's Not Easy)" Five for Fighting The Super Museum, Metropolis, Ill.: 70,000 items devoted to the Man of Steel, in a town actually named Metropolis.
"Gary, Indiana" from The Music Man City Methodist Church, Gary, Ind.: a nine-story Gothic ruin left behind by the steel industry's crash.
"Convoy" C.W. McCall Iowa 80 Truck Stop, Walcott, Iowa: the world's largest truck stop, complete with barber, dentist and trucking museum.
"Across the Universe" The Beatles Maharishi Vedic City, Iowa: a whole town built around Transcendental Meditation.
"Highway to Hell" AC/DC Hell, Michigan: for $100 you can be mayor for a day, and the job comes with horns.
"The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald" Gordon Lightfoot Great Lakes Shipwreck Museum, Paradise, Mich.: where the Fitzgerald's bell is remembered.
"Two Fish and an Elephant" Khruangbin The Big Fish Supper Club, Bena, Minn.: dinner beside a 65-foot muskie with very sharp teeth.
"Meet Me in St. Louis, Louis" Traditional (1904) City Museum, St. Louis: a ten-story playground of slides, tunnels and salvage, in the city of the 1904 World's Fair.
"Castles Made of Sand" The Jimi Hendrix Experience Harry Andrews' Chateau Laroche, Loveland, Ohio: a full-scale medieval castle one man built by hand.
"Evan Finds the Third Room" Khruangbin House on the Rock, Spring Green, Wis.: "an infinite-seeming collection of collections," with always another room.
"Satellite of Love" Lou Reed Sputnik IV Crash Site, Manitowoc, Wis.: where a chunk of Soviet satellite landed in the street in 1962.
"Cleveland Rocks" Ian Hunter "Welcome to Cleveland" Sign, Milwaukee: a rooftop prank confusing airline passengers since 1978.
Mid-Atlantic
"Yankee Doodle" Traditional Sussex Tavern at Rabbit's Ferry House, Lewes, Del.: colonial cocktails in a re-created 1740 tavern in the first town of the first state.
"So We Won't Forget" Khruangbin Iron Hill School No. 112C, Newark, Del.: a one-room schoolhouse preserving Delaware's segregated past.
"Secret Agent Man" Johnny Rivers National Cryptologic Museum, Fort Meade, Md.: the codebreaking gadgets that decided history.
"4th of July, Asbury Park (Sandy)" Bruce Springsteen Madam Marie's Psychic Booth, Asbury Park, N.J.: the boardwalk fortune-teller Springsteen wrote into this song.
"Main Title (Theme from Jaws)" John Williams Site of the 1916 Shark Attacks, Matawan, N.J.: the attacks a mile up a creek that helped inspire Jaws.
"Whiskey in the Jar" Thin Lizzy George Washington's Distillery, Alexandria, Va.: the first president's whiskey side hustle.
"Money (That's What I Want)" Barrett Strong The Mutilated Currency Division, Washington, D.C.: the federal office that refunds burned, chewed and laundered cash, even from inside a cow.
"Preamble" Schoolhouse Rock! The Preamble in License Plates, Washington, D.C.: "We the People," spelled out in vanity plates.
"Take Me Home, Country Roads" John Denver New River Gorge Bridge, Fayetteville, W.Va.: once a year on Bridge Day, people jump off it on purpose.
Northeast
"traitor" Olivia Rodrigo Annual Burning of Benedict Arnold, New London, Conn.: the town still burns its hometown traitor in effigy.
"A Horse with No Name" America The Desert of Maine, Freeport: 40 acres of sand in one of the greenest states.
"Cloudbusting" Kate Bush The Wilhelm Reich Museum, Rangeley, Maine: the home of the man this song is literally about, rain-making machine included.
"Blueberry Hill" Fats Domino Wild Blueberry Land, Columbia Falls, Maine: a theme park for the state fruit.
"Wild Horses" The Rolling Stones Ponyhenge, Lincoln, Mass.: a mysterious, ever-growing herd of rocking horses in a field.
"Stonehenge" Spinal Tap Mystery Hill: America's Stonehenge, Salem, N.H.: ancient site or wishful thinking? You decide.
"Wolfman's Brother" Phish Clark's Trading Post, Lincoln, N.H.: trained bears, a steam train, and the Wolfman, who chases it.
"Simple Gifts" Shaker hymn The First Shaker Village, Albany, N.Y.: the Shakers' first settlement, and the people who wrote this song.
"It's the End of the World as We Know It" R.E.M. Cobb's Hill, Rochester, N.Y.: where believers waited for the world to end in 1844. It didn't.
"Theme from Star Trek" Alexander Courage Star Trek Original Series Set Tour, Ticonderoga, N.Y.: the Enterprise bridge, rebuilt in an old supermarket by an Elvis impersonator.
"Umbrella" Rihanna feat. Jay-Z The Fantastic Umbrella Factory, Charlestown, R.I.: a 250-year-old farm turned hippie bazaar.
"Allentown" Billy Joel Carrie Furnaces, Pittsburgh: towering blast furnaces from Pennsylvania's steel age.
"Skating" Vince Guaraldi Trio Lake Morey Skate Trail, Fairlee, Vt.: the longest outdoor skate trail in the U.S.
Southeast & Florida
"Rocket Man" Elton John The Grave of Miss Baker, Huntsville, Ala.: America's first monkey to return alive from space. Bring a banana.
"Don't Worry, Be Happy" Bobby McFerrin Billy Bass Adoption Center, Little Rock, Ark.: where singing animatronic fish go to retire.
"Jesusland" Ben Folds Christ of the Ozarks, Eureka Springs, Ark.: a seven-story Jesus nicknamed "Our Milk Carton with Arms."
"About the Money" T.I. feat. Young Thug Trap Music Museum, Atlanta: T.I.'s museum, and the song the book says to play on the way there.
"My Old Kentucky Home" Stephen Foster Gallop to Glory, Louisville, Ky.: a hidden walk of fame of Derby-winning jockeys' handprints.
"Good Vibrations" The Beach Boys LIGO Livingston Observatory, La.: the instrument that first caught gravitational waves.
"Iko Iko" The Dixie Cups Mardi Gras World, New Orleans: the factory where the floats are built.
