item.title: Andrew Phung’s Favorite Calgary Spots
item.dc:creator: The Podcast Team
item.description:
Listen and subscribe on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and all major podcast apps.

Andrew Phung: My friend and I were in Calgary at the same time, and I was like, “Yo, let me take you out for dinner.” And I remember getting to his hotel, and he’s like, “How’d you get here so fast?” I’m like, “It’s Calgary. There’s not that much traffic.” He’s blown away. And we went to this restaurant, CHARCUT, get a table, and he’s like, “Did you make a reservation?” I’m like, “Nah, man, I just assume we get a table.” He’s like, “You just walked into a restaurant at 7:00 and got a table at this nice of a place?” I’m like, “Yeah, man.” He’s mind blown

Nora Richie: Ah, the Calgary life. No traffic, no reservations, no problem.

I’m Nora Ritchie, and this is Atlas Obscura, a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. This episode was produced in partnership with Travel Alberta. Explore Canada’s Wild Side.

This month, we’re talking with Canadian writers and artists who find inspiration in their home province of Alberta. Today, I’m talking with Andrew Phung. Andrew is a comedian and actor best known for playing Kimchee on Kim’s Convenience, and he’s the creator and star of Run the Burbs. But for this conversation, what matters most is that Andrew is a superfan of Calgary, the medium-sized city where he grew up.

This is an edited transcript of the Atlas Obscura Podcast: a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. Find the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and all major podcast apps.

Calgary is in southern Alberta, where the prairies meet the foothills of the Rocky Mountains. And to be honest, it’s not exactly considered the poster child for Alberta tourism. That honor usually goes to places like Banff and Lake Louise, with their turquoise lakes and mountain views. But Andrew thinks his hometown deserves a little more love.

Andrew: I would describe Calgary as a really big city that has all the amenities but feels a bit like a small town at times in regards to its friendliness. The mountains are right behind you. There’s really fresh air, and it is so bright. I think there’s some wild statistic, like Calgary gets the most sunshine in, like, all of the world during the winter or something like that.

Nora: I wanna hear about the street you grew up on, your neighborhood.

Andrew: I will talk about Northeast Calgary until I die. The northeast of Calgary is a quadrant of the city. It is the most culturally diverse. I grew up in Whitehorn, Temple, Falconridge, Coral Springs. I’ll name the neighborhoods, but Coral Springs was where we ended up last.

And what I loved about it was, Coral Springs is full of dreamers. It’s people who this was the first new house they bought. And it was really affordable to new immigrants, families starting out fresh. So literally everyone on my street had kids, and so we were always playing. Like, every day after school, we’d come home, we would get on our bikes, we would go to someone’s house, get the baseball equipment, get the hockey equipment, carry the net, you know, all that stuff.

Every day at 5:00, you know, people would come home from work, and then we’d have to go inside and have dinner and do homework. That was our street. It felt a little bit like Pleasantville.

Nora: It does sound like Pleasantville. So your parents are Chinese and Vietnamese. How did they end up in Calgary?

Andrew: So most people assume your parents come to Canada together. My parents met in Canada. They had different immigration stories. My mom immigrated to Airdrie, Alberta, which is a suburb of Calgary. My dad ended up in Saskatchewan. A church there had sponsored a bunch of Vietnamese refugees into Canada.

And then my dad tracked down a friend living in Calgary, and he went to take the bus to Calgary and waited for him at the bus station, and the guy didn’t show up. And then my dad saw another person delivering Chinese food, went and talked to that guy, and that guy took my dad home, and my dad lived with him for two years.

The Asian community in Calgary in the ’70s and ’80s was so tight-knit. Like, if they saw one of their own, they would take you in. It was so supportive. And I remember years later, my dad saw an old friend. I’m like, “Yo, who was that guy?” My dad’s like, “Oh, I used to live with him.” And I’m like, “You need to give me the full backstory on that.”

But my mom and dad met in Airdrie at a card game. My uncle introduced my mom and dad, and I was born and raised in Calgary. That’s our immigration story, and I really always reflect on how welcoming Canada was in the ’70s and ’80s. Really welcoming in refugees and immigrants to build a better life.

And my parents always say, “Andrew, we’re living the Canadian dream. Everything we do is the Canadian dream.”

Nora: Related to your work in comedy and growing up, was there a time in your childhood that you were sort of like, “Wait a minute, I’m pretty funny. Like, people think I’m funny. Maybe I should explore this more?”

Andrew: Growing up as an Asian person in Calgary, comedy and the arts isn’t really an avenue you pursue. And so even though I was very outgoing, I went to university for a degree in economics, with a focus on oil and gas. I thought I was gonna work in oil and gas. I thought I was gonna become a lawyer, like that was the route I was gonna take.

The only person I saw that was Asian in the media was, like, Jackie Chan, Jet Li later on. In Canada, there’s a show called Degrassi, and we had a character named Yick. He was the only Asian character on Degrassi: Junior High and Degrassi High. He didn’t get a lot of stories, but when Yick was there it was like, “Yo, Yick was there. He was at the party.”

Nora: I sadly only know that show from Drake.

Andrew: Yeah. So I didn’t see myself in it, so I didn’t think it was an option. It wasn’t until high school when I took drama in high school as an option, I really enjoyed it, and I joined the high school improv team. And even then, like, I was like, “I’m probably not gonna do this very long,” Because I sucked. I sucked so much.

Nora: Yeah, when you say you sucked, what makes you say that?

Andrew: So I grew up watching a lot of Saturday Night Live and Conan O’Brien and, and David Letterman, and so I was trying to be too funny. And I think that was one of the things in comedy I learned early on, that you shouldn’t try to be funny, you should just find your comedic voice, and I didn’t understand that.

So I was trying to mimic Sandler and Farley and Will Ferrell and Cheri Oteri and Ana Gasteyer. I was trying to mimic those people when I should’ve been just trying to find my own voice. So I wasn’t very good at it cause my timing was so off.

I didn’t know what my voice was, and it wasn’t until my drama teacher, Loretta Beesh, encouraged me to go down to the Loose Moose Theatre Company, and the Loose Moose Theatre Company trained me for free. I showed up as a 15-year-old kid. We came down with my friends, we took the bus there, they never charged us for a class. They trained us for free. I performed at Loose Moose Theatre from 1999 until now whenever I’m back in Calgary. Until I started making Kim's Convenience, I was playing at Loose Moose Theatre.

Nora: Oh, wow.

Andrew: Everything I know about the arts and, and, and performing in the arts, building arts, creating in the arts, is from the Loose Moose Theatre.

Nora: Is there any kind of moment from those early days that still sticks with you?

Andrew: Yeah. I remember I got picked to do a show, and I was not very good that night. And again, early on, I’m 16, 17, I don’t have a comedic voice. But when you fail when you’re 16 or 17, it’s like the end of the world. Because school teaches you to be right and to be perfect and to get good grades.

So I felt like I had the worst show, and I’d let everyone down, and I remember my artistic director, Dennis Cahill, who’s still the artistic director, said, “Oh, tonight was a rough show.” But he put it very bluntly. He didn’t sugarcoat it. And he said, “Tonight was a rough show. Well, you get to come back next week and do it again.”

And just hearing that, it was like, “Oh, it’s not over. I get to come back and do this again.” And I think that mentality and that ability to fail has shaped everything, every ounce of who I am today. The willingness to fail. That moment changed everything for me.

Nora: That’s an incredible attitude to have as an artist, of course. You know, Calgary isn’t necessarily known as a comedy town, although maybe a little bit now from you, but what do you think it was about it, about the Loose Moose or about Calgary that allowed that kind of space to take root?

Andrew: Well, firstly, I think Calgary has a very underappreciated reputation as a comedy town, because Bruce McCullough and Mark McKinney from the Kids in the Hall came from Loose Moose Theatre. The Kids in the Hall are foundational in comedy, I think, I believe, in the world in the ’90s. And two of their members came from Loose Moose Theatre.

But the thing about Calgary is that it is not Toronto, it is not Vancouver, it is not LA. So I believe that the people who pursued comedy in Calgary did it for the pure love of the game. They love comedy. They have jobs. We all had a side job, we all had hustles that we were trying to do.

You perform at these gigs and these venues that pay dozens of dollars on your best night because you love it. It’s less about the success. So that’s why I think Calgary is such a wonderful space for artists, because you do it ’cause you love it.

Nora: I know you from Kimchee on Kim’s Convenience, which is such great comfort food of a show. And then of course from Run the Burbs. I wanna talk a little bit about that, ’cause that’s really, you know, your baby. And it’s set outside Calgary too, right?

Andrew: We were trying to shoot it in Calgary, but it’s set in a suburb that is reflective of Calgary.

Nora: So tell me about that process and what parts of your own life you bring into making that show?

Andrew: When I was on Kim’s Convenience, I was always like, ”What’s the next thing?” And I was always, like, watching the showrunners, Ins and Kevin, make things, and directors, and I’m like, ”Oh, this is interesting.” So I started kind of plotting on what’s my next idea, what’s my next thing? And my co-creator and I, Scott Townend and I, my buddy, like he was one of my best friends, we were coming up with ideas, and we just started putting together ideas of a TV show we wanted to see.

And we wanted to see something that was about a family in this day and age. I wanted to see a diverse family. Kim’s Convenience was about the immigrant experience, and then Run the Burbs is about the experience of the children of those immigrants. I want to see them thrive. I also wanted to showcase families of color thriving, and that often happens in the suburbs, and I saw that growing up in Calgary.

In Calgary, the suburbs is where a lot of immigrant families and newcomers are thriving. It is a chance for them to have a backyard. It is a chance for them to have a barbecue with hamburgers and hot dogs. And so I really brought that energy to Run the Burbs. We wanted the family to be reflective of the families I see in the suburbs.

And I want to see families that had honest conversations with their kids, and that were inclusive of their kids, and to have emotionally intelligent parents and kids just trying to be better. And so it was a lot of, what I see in parenting around me and how I work as a father.

Nora: Yeah. I mean, you also made that important choice to set it in Calgary. Why did you wanna set it in Calgary?

Andrew: Well, first I want to set it in Calgary ’cause we never see Calgary. We never see modern Calgary.

Alberta is beautiful for landscapes. And so many of our Westerns are shot in Calgary and Alberta. It’s beautiful. I love it. There’s entire towns dedicated to being Westerns. But I wanted to showcase Calgary as a modern city, so I wanted to showcase Calgary as Calgary.

Nora: What was it like having it be your own creative baby? Like there had to be some really challenging parts about it. Could you speak a little bit about that?

Andrew: Making your own TV show is a miracle. It’s an absolute challenge. Everything has to break right. There are so many talented people who are relying on years of experience and knowledge. It’s literally hundreds of thousands of hours of experience that goes into one day of television. So making it is a miracle. Dealing with network notes, budget constraints, schedules, weather—all the technical pieces. Your camera has to go.

Everything has to break right for you to get through the day, and so it is such a challenge. And I’m so thankful for the experience, but when I finished making Run the Burbs, I was like, “Oh, my God. I can breathe again. Oh, the pain, the stress.”

It takes years off your life, I feel like. Though at the same time, I was so creatively fulfilled. I loved making it. I miss it so much.

Nora: I’m putting you on the spot here, but are there any spots if someone’s visiting Calgary for the first time and you’re like, they gotta go to this restaurant or this theater or this, like hike or whatever?

Andrew: I will always recommend Loose Moose Theatre, but I think if you’re gonna spend an afternoon in Calgary, 17th Avenue SW is so much fun. I was down there recently. I walked down there and I met up with a friend at Class Clown, for hamburgers, and everyone had been hyping it up, and it was worth the hype.

Class Clown burgers are incredible. Then we walked over to From Another, which is this vintage shop that is in Calgary, Edmonton, and Vancouver, but they got a great spot in Calgary. We walked down the street to Less 17, but along the way are tons of bars and pubs, and along the way on 17th Avenue, we passed by this vintage market that just popped up on the street.

17th Avenue SW is such a great walkable area. Kensington is also a lovely area as well, but I would encourage people to spend an afternoon in the northeast of Calgary. And again, you need a car to do that. Calgary is, I acknowledge it is not the most walkable city, but I think the food in the northeast of Calgary, and when you head off into the southeast of Calgary, like 17th Avenue SE, it is the most authentic food you can get.

Like the best banh mi sandwich I’ll ever have is in Calgary. I tell people about it. I get DMs on my Instagram all the time from people being like, “Yo, I was in Calgary for work, and I went and got this banh mi. You’re absolutely right.” I had a friend write me again. They’re like, “I went there three times, Andrew.”

Calgary, when you break it down and look for things, there is a pace of life, and there are so many things to explore that are worth it. As a parent, I always tell people Calgary is so family-friendly. You have the Science Center, but then you also, surrounding Calgary, you have all these like corn mazes and little areas that have popped up in Calaway Park that are such wonderful parks and places for kids to be.

And then inside the city, there’s so much to do because we have space. Again, there’s all these warehouses that have been converted into batting cages and play places. I just think it has all the elements of a big city, all the perks. Beautiful hotels, landmarks, art, things to do, without like the, the, the hustle and bustle and busyness of a Toronto. You know? Getting anywhere in Toronto, you accept it for all of its flaws.

Nora: That reminds me, I live in New York, but I went to Madison, Wisconsin recently for something, and I was like, “Where, where is everybody? What’s going on?”

This is what it is. It’s just a quieter pace. There’s less people on the street. It’s not so busy. But it was a really lovely place. It's a nice change of pace.

Andrew: Yeah, definitely. Nice change of pace. Things are easy to do. Oh, I can stop and breathe for a second, which is very nice.

Nora: Well, thank you, Andrew. I really appreciate your time.

Andrew: Yeah. Thank you for chatting with me.

item.title: 8 Gargoyles and Grotesques Hiding in Plain Sight
item.dc:creator: Holyn Thigpen
item.description:
What’s more wondrous than towering spires on a building? Stained glass? Vaulted windows, or garden roofs? One word: Ghouls. Nothing jazzes up a normal old cathedral or mansion more than a mischievous face etched in stone, smiling (or, more likely, grimacing) at those passing below. Gargoyles and grotesques, in their own endearingly ugly way, are one of the best ways for architects to let their creations stand apart from the pack and inspire reflection for centuries to come.

While most of these creatures are made in a similar style, with recognizable bodily features, expressions, and poses, there are a handful around the globe that are unapologetically unique: sometimes familiar, sometimes offbeat, and always worth a closer look.

A Note on Gargoyles vs. Grotesques

Both are ornate stone figures carved into buildings; however, gargoyles also double as waterspouts to drain rainwater off a building, whereas grotesques are purely decorative.


1. Darth Vader Grotesque - Washington, D.C.

D.C.’s National Cathedral is the largest in the U.S. and the sixth largest in the world, but it has another, less obvious claim to fame: a small carving of Darth Vader among its spires. When the cathedral underwent constuction in the 1980s, it held a contest for schoolchildren to submit designs, and this infamous villain took third place, earning it a spot on the exterior. For the best view of the Dark Lord, grab your binoculars and head to the northwest parking lot. Near the top of the northwest tower, Vader is just above a large skull.

2. House with Chimaeras - Kyiv, Ukraine

Polish-Ukrainian architect Vladislav Gorodetsky, “the Gaudí, of Ukraine,” intended for this animal-themed building to be his permanent residence; however, he was forced to vacate it when his pocketbook ran dry. The house, located in Kyiv’s historic Lypky neighborhood, is right across the street from the Ukrainian president’s office and has been used for diplomatic ceremonies since 2005. Its gargoyles and grotesques were inspired by Gorodetsky’s love of hunting, and inside is even filled with stuffed versions of many of these same animals.

3. Plein Rond de Eik - Amersfoort, Netherlands

Architect Changiz Tehrani designed this mixed-use structure with 22 different WhatsApp emoji faces that stare out at passersby, including fan favorites like the smile, the wink, the heart eyes, the kissy face, and the winking face with tongue out. Tehrani drew inspiration from an Amsterdam building called “The House with the Heads,” which depicts the faces of six Greek gods.

4. The Policeman Grotesque - Carlisle, England

An officer who died in the line of duty is memorialized on the south-facing outer wall of Carlisle Cathedral, surprisingly inconspicuous beside the medieval gargoyles and grotesques. Police Constable George Russell’s stone likeness wears a helmet and star badge, marking his life’s dedication to service and safety. Russell is buried in Carlisle and also honored by a plaque at the Oxenholme Lake District railway station.

5. The Bull of Santa Maria del Fiore - Florence, Italy

Among the Duomo’s many easy-to-miss intricacies is this stone bull’s head facing Via Ricasoli and right over the Porta della mandorla, the door that allows one up into the grand dome. There are two explanations for the bull’s origin: One holds that it was the builders’ tribute to the draft animals used to construct the cathedral. The other (far more fun) theory is that a stonemason designed the bull to look straight into the shop of his girlfriend’s husband, a daily reminder that it was the stonemason she truly loved.

6. The Vampire Rabbit of Newcastle - Newcastle upon Tyne, England

For over a century, this deformed rabbit has sat at the back of St. Nicholas Cathedral, but no one can say why or how it came to be. Some say it represents the coming of spring (à la the Easter Bunny), whereas others insist it was built to scare away grave robbers. Still others believe the creature was intended to be a normal rabbit but, unfortunately, its ears were accidentally put on backward.

7. ‘Alien’ Gargoyle - Paisley, Scotland

When Paisley Abbey underwent renovations in 1993, 13 of its gargoyles were removed and replaced with updated versions, though one of the stonemasons on the job took some major creative liberties. His contribution to the facade looks strikingly like H.R. Giger's Xenomorph from the “Alien” franchise, though it’s never been confirmed whether this was his exact intention or a happy coincidence.

8. Park Grove Manor - Oak Park, Illinois

E.E. Roberts designed a number of homes in this sleepy Chicago suburb, working in styles that ranged from Victorian to Tudor to Prairie. Perhaps his most fanciful building, Park Grove Manor is adorned with playful, chubby-faced gargoyles and grotesques. Above the service entrances to the building are sculptures depicting an architect and a bricklayer, both of them amusingly cartoonish. This may have been Roberts becoming less self-serious in his older age, joyfully deriding the pretensions of modern architecture.

item.title: Only-in-Anchorage Winter Traditions
item.dc:creator: Holyn Thigpen
item.description:
Winter brings out the best of Anchorage. Under a blanket of snow, the city comes alive with festivals exploring regional history, lively tributes to Indigenous culture, decades-old sled dog races, and comfort food best enjoyed with friends and family. Here, Alaska’s adventurous spirit is felt in the traditions of diverse communities and seasonal occasions that offer a little something for everyone. Whether you’re taking in the shimmering colors of the aurora borealis from a snowmobile or enjoying films by up-and-coming artists at the Bear Tooth Theatrepub, there’s no shortage of events to make a winter in Anchorage one for the books.

Heyi Days

Nov. 27-Dec. 31, 2026

Translating to “winter” in Dena’ina Athabascan, the name of this month-long celebration honors Anchorage’s First People — “heyi” is the Dena’ina word for winter. It’s prime time to enjoy winter outdoors, check out local arts markets, and enjoy seasonal community events like solstice. There’s also delicious food left and right, from Alaska halibut tacos to Himalayan curries and steamed dumplings best enjoyed by an outdoor fire. While unique events unfold each day, the whole city comes alive with lights and music. Many parks host ice rinks and ski loops, some of which give you an up-close look at Anchorage’s wildlife, from moose to hares to foxes.

Anchorage International Film Festival

Dec. 4-13, 2026

Alaska’s biggest celebration of independent film is a can’t-miss event for filmmakers and cinephiles alike. Along with screenings of short and feature-length projects, guests can attend Q&A sessions and panel discussions or participate in workshops and networking events. While artists from all over the world screen their works here, the festival is especially focused on growing and sustaining Alaska’s film community, as well as providing a greater platform for Indigenous voices.

Solstice Tree Tour

Dec. 12, 2026

Hosted by the Nordic Skiing Association of Anchorage, this winter solstice celebration turns Kincaid Park into a winter wonderland, with visitors passing dozens of decorated trees and colorful lights in the park’s Mize Loop (just remember your skis or snowshoes!). After finishing the 1.5-mile loop, guests are encouraged to grab free hot chocolate and s’mores, enjoy live music, and vote on their favorite tree. Younger attendees can crawl through illuminated tunnels set up throughout the park while adults sip drinks from Raven’s Ring Brewery by the warming barrels.

Anchorage Folk Festival

Jan. 21-31, 2027

For 37 years and counting, this free event has showcased up-and-coming artists and helped build community through music. During “Folk Week,” venues around town host local and visiting artists, while music workshops are held on the weekends at University of Alaska Anchorage’s Wendy Williamson Auditorium. There are many other folksy events to participate in, too, from a barn dance to a ukulele jam to a banjo contest. Also, an annual fundraiser concert helps support future editions of the festival, with tickets starting at $20.

Alaska Craft Brew & Barley Wine Festival

Jan. 30, 2027

Anchorage is a city that loves its brews, so it’s only right that they be celebrated! Each year, the Brewers Guild of Alaska partners with Peak 2 Peak Events to host this epic ode to beers, ciders, wines, meads, and more. Award-winning brewers from across the state converge at the Dena’ina Center for a day of beverage tasting, hearty grub, games, and live music. Over 200 different drinks are available to try, including a wide selection of nonalcoholic options. Plus, there’s a chance to take home fun swag like beanies, socks, koozies, and stainless-steel pint glasses.

Fur Rendezvous

Feb. 25-March 7, 2027

For more than 90 years, “Fur Rondy” has brought Anchorage to life with events and activities all over the city. The festival is inspired by the rendezvous that Alaska’s fur trappers and miners had each winter, sharing stories and drinks after months of isolation in the wilderness. Fur Rondy celebrates the region’s unique history through all kinds of annual traditions, from sled dog races to snow sculptures to the Frostbite Footrace (where wintery costumes are encouraged). The fest is even home to the world’s largest Outhouse Races, which requires teams to push festive latrines through a race course.

Iditarod Sled Dog Race

March 6, 2027

Each year, hundreds of dogs gear up on the first Saturday of March for the ceremonial start of the “Last Great Race on Earth”: a 1,000-mile course that starts on 4th Avenue and D Street in downtown Anchorage and goes all the way to Nome. There are plenty of spots around town to watch the action, from Cordova Street and 16th Avenue (the steepest hill of the day) to the scenic University Lake near the University of Alaska Anchorage campus. Also, many mushers open up their kennels to the public for tours (and sometimes even tutorials!) all year long.

Aurora Viewing

August-April

Anchorage is the perfect place to take in the awesome beauty of the aurora borealis, a.k.a. the northern lights, with prime viewing locations all over the city. From Point Woronzof, a coastal park on the northwestern edge of town, to the Eagle River Nature Center at one of the entrances to Chugach State Park, you can easily pick and choose the viewing experience that works best for you. There are also numerous tour services to help visitors make the most of their Anchorage winter experience, including adventures that combine the lights with dogsledding and snowmobiling.

item.title: Anchorage: A City Within the Wild
item.dc:creator: Holyn Thigpen
item.description:
In Anchorage, exploring nature isn’t only for a rare free day or a well-planned vacation; it’s a part of daily life, as integral to the city as its infrastructure and cultural offerings. A day here may start with a morning walk on any of the hundreds of miles of trails, continue with freshly caught salmon for lunch at a restaurant with coastal views, and end with a sunset picnic on a rocky outcropping, where the only sounds are crashing waves and the fleeting glimpses of beluga whales.

Located on a coastal plain that shifts into alpine slopes farther east, Anchorage is unique in how its different ecosystems overlap, creating rich diversity in wildlife, botany, and geology. You can experience the best of nature while still enjoying all the creature comforts of urban life and stumble across breathtaking sights without even looking for them. In this guide, we’ve given you some starting points for exploring the wild from Alaska’s biggest city, with wonders ranging from undisturbed wooded trails to marshes that all kinds of animals call home. Ready to take a walk on the wild side?

Ship Creek

This 25-mile-long river flows from the Chugach Mountains down into the Port of Alaska on Anchorage’s northern side, where it’s become a popular spot for sport fishing and bird watching. Thanks to its mud and sedge flats, and ocean-fed waters, this area is home to a massive annual run of coho and Chinook salmon. In fact, it’s the only urban Chinook fishery in the world.

The 5.8-mile Ship Creek Trail is a perfect way to spend time in nature without leaving the city limits, providing views of salmon spawning and swimming upstream during the summer. Stops along the way, like Ship Creek Overlook Park and the pedestrian bridge just off King’s Landing, provide especially great panoramas of the river and the surrounding mountains. It’s not uncommon to see anglers trying their luck for 20- to 30-pound salmon, and you can even visit the statue of Dena’ina matriarch Grandma Olga, fish filets in her hands and a bronze drying rack behind her.

Tony Knowles Coastal Trail

For a longer walk, try this 11-mile path that stretches from downtown Anchorage all the way to the Kincaid Park Chalet. However, if you’re looking for a shorter trek, have no fear: The trail is accessible from multiple points in the city, meaning you can hop on or off. You don’t have to explore on foot either, as the trail can be traversed easily by bike and, in the winter, cross-country skis. No matter how you travel the trail, you’re guaranteed some incredible views of downtown Anchorage, Mount McKinley (Denali), Mount Susitna, and Fire Island, especially as you reach the hills near Point Woronzof.

The trail offers a rare chance to pass through a number of different biomes, as it winds through marsh, muskeg (acidic, waterlogged peatland), and thick spruce forest. There’s also plenty of wildlife nearby, with moose, in particular, enjoying long walks on the path during the winter. Other animals often spotted include sandhill cranes, ermine, bald eagles, and even beluga whales in Cook Inlet, so don’t forget your camera.

Kincaid Park

For even more great hiking, visit Kincaid Park, a 1,400-acre green space that was once a Cold War missile base. There’s plenty to do in Kincaid: walk down the 40 miles of cleared trails, practice archery on a designated range, paddle through Little Campbell Lake, or play disc golf on an 18-hole course. There are also seven different soccer fields, a motocross course, and a giant sand dune with stunning views of Cook Inlet and the Kenai Peninsula. In the winter, the park becomes a premier destination for sledding and cross-country skiing, with trails for every skill level.

Potter Marsh

Just 15 minutes south of downtown, this part of the Anchorage Coastal Wildlife Refuge is one of the best wildlife viewing spots in all of Alaska, offering sweeping vistas of the Turnagain Arm tidal waterway and half a mile of boardwalk across the channels and sedges. This wetland ecosystem is full of creatures big and small, from muskrats paddling through the water to the occasional moose taking a dip. And birders, rejoice: The marsh is home to more than 130 bird species, including Arctic tern, Canada geese, trumpeter swans, red-necked grebes, and northern pintails.

Pro tip: Visit in April for the greatest variety of migrating birds, or in midsummer to see three different species of salmon schooling under the boardwalk. Information panels and telescopes along the path make it easy to enjoy a self-guided tour and take in the sights and sounds of the marsh at your own pace. You can also see the marsh from aboard the Alaska Railroad or while driving down the Seward Highway.

Beluga Point

Also along the Seward Highway sits Beluga Point, a rocky promontory named for the population of beluga whales that can be spotted each July and August when they come to catch salmon in the inlet. However, no matter what time of year you visit, 180-degree views of the Chugach Mountains make this a worthwhile place to stop and take in your surroundings.

Nearly every day, the Turnagain Arm bore tide — a dramatic wave caused by incoming tides — sweeps through the inlet. At a height of 6 to 10 feet, it’s one of the largest bore tides in the world, and because it’s relatively slow moving, surfers from all over the globe come to tackle it.

Flattop Mountain

The most-climbed mountain in Alaska is just east of Anchorage in Chugach State Park, accessible from the Glen Alps Trailhead (reachable by a shuttle that leaves from downtown Anchorage). It’s a 1.5-mile hike from the trail parking lot to the top of the plateau, with an elevation gain of 1,500 feet and incredible views of the Anchorage skyline, as well as Denali, Mount Foraker and Mount Spurr on clear days. For an even greater challenge, visitors can make their way up an additional trail to the peak, though this is a steep journey best suited for experienced outdoor adventurers.

Aside from hiking, Flattop is a popular destination for berry picking in the summer and fall, with its trails (especially the Powerline Pass) taking you past wild blueberries, crowberries, and lowbush cranberries. The summit of Flattop is also a hub for paragliders, with its level surface and multidirectional open areas allowing for many possible setups (and plenty of photo ops).

With all this and more to explore, what are you waiting for? Embark on your Anchorage adventure today!

item.title: Where to See the World’s Creepiest Dolls and Toys
item.dc:creator: Holyn Thigpen
item.description:
Humans have played with dolls for thousands of years, but it was not until the 18th century, when improved manufacturing rendered them more lifelike, that they started to be seen as sinister. Doll makers pivoted to porcelain skin, glass eyes, and wigs made of human hair, creating children and babies whose uncanniness to real people made them more unnerving than lovable. Later, in the Victorian Era, “mourning dolls” became a common way to remember deceased children, wearing their clothes and even sitting atop their coffins. Throw in Chucky, Annabelle, Slappy the Dummy, and numerous other evil dolls from pop culture, and boom: Dolls = creepy.

At these places around the world, dolls and other eerie toys are the main attraction. Some spots are happy-go-lucky art projects that, despite their creator’s intentions, still have the power to unsettle visitors. Others were always shrouded in darkness, created to showcase murders and mysteries. All of them are excellent examples of the creativity — and lore — that a single toy can embody, as well as our enduring fascination with the uncanny and ever-so-slightly “off.”

1. Tombées du Camion - Saint-Ouen, France

This tiny shop just outside Paris specializes in vintage objects from French factories, the odder the better. The name of the store (which translates to “goods that have fallen off the back of a truck”) is perhaps the first sign that this isn’t your average antique store; inside, you’ll find ephemera ranging from glass dolls’ eyes to coffin handles to bicycle-shaped sunglasses, with items sorted into small wooden boxes or attached to the ceiling.

The owner, sculptor and interior designer Charles Mas, wanted to give visitors the chance to find all the toys, tools, and trinkets they enjoyed as children. “I focus on objects that have no market value, but an emotional and nostalgic value,” he says. “Many things that, without imagination, are worthless.”

2. Ospedale delle Bambole - Rome, Italy

For close to 90 years, the Squatriti family has pieced broken dolls back together from this small shop in Rome’s Centro Storico. Inside, benches and shelves are cluttered with various body parts, while the work tables are filled with paintbrushes, twine, and plaster. Each year, the Squatritis save upwards of 1,000 period pieces: not only dolls, but also vases, statuettes, plates, and more. The shop’s owner, Federico Squatriti, says that the “hospital” has changed very little since his relatives first opened it. At that time, the Squatritis lived above the shop, and as a boy, Federico would drop in to say hello to his father, uncle, and grandmother while they worked. Locals have referred to the space as a “shop of terror,” but to the entire Squatriti family, it is a second home.

3. Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death - Baltimore, Maryland

Back in the mid 20th century, when forensic science was still in its infancy, Chicago socialite Frances Glessner Lee created 20 dioramas of real-life crime scenes on a 1-inch-to-1-foot scale. To ensure accuracy, Lee attended autopsies for all the cases and re-created their settings with astonishing detail. (One even contains a hanging wall calendar for the year of the crime.) She called her project the Nutshell Studies because of the purported purpose of a forensic investigation: to “convict the guilty, clear the innocent, and find the truth in a nutshell.”

At Harvard’s Magrath Library of Legal Medicine, Lee led seminars in which she guided students through the dioramas, helping them draw conclusions about the crime based on the information displayed. After she passed away in 1962, the Nutshell collection was obtained by the Maryland Office of the Chief Medical Examiner and fully restored. Today, the models are still used for educational purposes by investigators.

4. The House of Dreams Museum - London, England

The lavishly designed home of textile designer and art director Stephen Wright also serves as a museum of his work, with Wright residing in his upstairs flat even while guests wander the halls below. The entire ground floor of the home (including its garden and exterior) exists as one exquisite sculpture of mosaics, collages, dolls, and handwritten “memory boards,” showcasing all of Wright’s loves and losses. He started transforming the home in 1992 as a side project, but after the death of his partner and his parents in quick succession, it became an outlet for his grief. Even today, the space is evolving, with Wright adding bits and pieces donated by visitors or discovered at flea markets.

5. Mary’s Gone Wild Folk Art and Doll Baby Museum - Supply, North Carolina

According to artist Mary Paulsen, God commissioned her to give her collection of 6,000 dolls a proper home, complete with painted windows, tin cans, glass shards, and whatever other scraps and goods neighbors have donated. Mary will gladly transform anything she’s given into “gonna-make-you-smile art” for the village, which consists of a little red schoolhouse, soda pop shoppe, library, and chapel (where she herself got married). She also sells some of her pieces, with all proceeds going to Feed the Children, a nonprofit fighting childhood food insecurity.

While the village may be a bit unsettling at first, most visitors quickly warm up to the cheerful whimsy of Mary’s vision. In fact, Mary is often around to greet visitors and will drop whatever she’s working on to give a tour and introduce you to the dolls. “Mary is a delight to talk with and her place is incredibly creative,” one visitor reflected. “A lot of junk…lovingly presented!”

6. Hospital de Bonecas - Lisbon, Portugal

Opened in 1830, this is one of the world’s oldest doll repair shops, and it has the collection to prove it. Over its nearly two centuries of operation, any doll that’s gone unclaimed has been kept by the shop proprietors in their “museum,” which also holds a slew of different body parts sorted in drawers, miniature furniture pieces, and costumes hung on a clothesline. The shop designs many of these doll clothes itself and also makes toy cars, planes, and carousels.

7. Lost Toys of the Nybohov Funicular - Stockholm, Sweden

This underground cable railway has connected Liljeholmen and the Nybohov hill since 1964, but no one knows exactly when dozens of toys started turning up there. Still, locals have grown quite fond of these colorful additions to the dark tunnel, so much so that when authorities tried to remove them in 2012, Stockholm residents protested, demanding the plushies be left in peace. Their efforts paid off: The nearly 30 toys still adorn the metal rails and concrete walls of the funicular, waving hello to any children who pass.

8. Doll’s Head Trail - Atlanta, Georgia

In Atlanta’s Constitution Lakes nature preserve, a strange pathway winds through the wetlands and forest. Doll arms rise from the ground holding toy cars, with a nearby brick reading “Giving daddy a hand.” Clothed dolls lean against tree trunks, their heads replaced by rusty tools. One baby’s face sits atop a board that says “fashion” in neon paint, while another is positioned among mossy bricks and pinecones.

This collection of oddities was created by Joel Slaton, a local carpenter who wanted to repurpose discarded materials he found in the area. Soon, others started contributing their own art pieces, with one caveat: Every work must be made of things from inside the park itself. Bringing things with you is strongly discouraged, with a sign at the trailhead explaining that “litter makes the angels cry.”

9. Robert the Doll - Key West, Florida

In the early 20th century, young Gene Otto received this straw-filled doll and, naming it Robert, started bringing it with him everywhere he went. It wasn’t long before Gene’s family heard him having full conversations alone in his room and screaming in the middle of the night. Later, when furniture was mysteriously upturned, Gene blamed it on Robert. Some visitors to the Otto family home even heard high-pitched giggling and spotted a doll-like figure in the window.

Gene has long since passed away, but Robert is still around, living happily at the Fort East Martello Museum in Key West, Florida. You can visit him here, but beware: He’s known to curse those who take his photo without asking permission first.

10. Burke & Hare Murder Dolls - Edinburgh, Scotland

Nearly a decade after “Anatomy Murderers” William Burke and William Hare terrorized Edinburgh, these 17 dolls were found in a city park, each one nested in a miniature coffin. Rumors arose that the figures were effigies of the duo’s victims, though other folks theorized they depicted local sailors who had never received a proper burial. Regardless of who they were meant to represent, the dolls were most likely crafted by a cobbler, as they’re made from the profession’s special hinges and nails.

11. Doll Garden of Sabile - Sabile, Latvia

Hundreds of straw dolls go about their regular lives in this large garden: cutting down trees, cooking meals, riding bikes, and sawing wood. They were all crafted by the garden’s owner, Daina Kučere, whose answer to why she made the village is more or less “Why not?” Residents wear all kinds of attire, from police uniforms to wedding dresses to baggy sweats (really just whatever Kučere digs up). Anyone can pass through the garden at their leisure and show their support by dropping a few coins in the central donation box.

12. Miyoshi Mononoke Museum - Miyoshi, Japan

Japan’s first public museum dedicated to yokai (the supernatural spirits and monsters of Japanese folklore) contains over 5,000 artifacts, including many dolls and action figures depicting the quirky creatures. There’s even an interactive room full of yokai-related activity stations, where guests can use light projections to make images move and change, or color their own yokai, which then appear as animations on a screen. The “yokai camera” is another fun element to try out, letting visitors take selfies inside a historic yokai picture scroll and transform into yokai themselves.

13. Aunt Claudia’s Dolls - Juneau, Alaska

Shortly after World War II, artist and toy collector Claudia Kelsey moved to Juneau with her family of dolls and figurines. By the time she passed away 60 years later, her collection had grown to number in the hundreds, and her close friend decided to open it up to the public as a gallery.

While Claudia was especially focused on finding handmade Alaskan Indigenous dolls, her collection included items from all over the world. Since the gallery opened in 2010, it has received donations from doll enthusiasts in Greenland, Scandinavia, Russia, and more, showcasing many different methods and materials used by doll makers. In fact, the gallery’s director and curator, Mary Ellen Frank, is a maker herself, crafting figurines of Alaska Native leaders and elders using traditional carving techniques.

14. Beaver Island Toy Museum - Beaver Island, Michigan

On a small isle in the middle of Lake Michigan lives this colorful (and slightly creepy) toy collection, with items ranging from doll heads in jars to midcentury action figures to a big jar of tacks. The space is small, so items are arranged creatively, with old bicycles hanging from the rafters and toy cars and planes glued to the walls. The toys also flow into the yard: an endearing hodgepodge of overgrown potted plants, colorful deck chairs, and stone animal sculptures. In the back shed, local artists’ work is exhibited, including a photo series of Bigfoot lounging about the toy museum and island.

Even in her 80s, the museum’s founder, Mary Rose, can be found greeting visitors most days and still maintains her expert eye for toy curation. Start chatting with her and she may just show you some of her son’s artwork, or steer you toward the perfect toy to take home.

15. The Troll Hole - Alliance, Ohio

Since 2014, owner Sherry Groom has shared her love of Scandinavia’s ugly, mountain-dwelling folk creatures at this elaborate museum, which features a grotto, waterfalls, and naturally, a 10-foot troll mountain. In 2012, Sherry took home the Guinness record for World’s Largest Troll Collection, and it’s pretty easy to see why: Everywhere you look are rows and rows of trolls, from the smiley, wild-haired dolls created in the 1950s to rare ninja trolls and a vintage Trollmobile. The Troll Hole also features a coffee shop, The Grumpy Troll Cafe, and hosts meet-and-greets with the “Trolls” movie character, Queen Poppy, every Sunday.

item.title: Where to See the World’s Most Famous Preserved Body Parts
item.dc:creator: Holyn Thigpen
item.description:
Sure, you’ve seen a dead body before, but have you ever seen a thumb preserved in salt? How about a saint’s heart shrouded in gold?

Beyond the normal displays of skeletons in medical museums and holy leaders’ bodies in churches and temples, there’s a whole world of bits and pieces to explore. Throughout history, body parts have been taken as trophies during wartime, worshipped as miraculous healing agents, cut off and displayed to honor their owners, or simply saved incidentally by natural processes.

If seeing a whole body feels banal, we recommend delving from the complete corpse to its components. Here are some of our favorites from around the world.

1. National Museum of Health and Medicine - Silver Spring, Maryland

Among the 24 million medical instruments and anatomical specimens housed here are portions of Abraham Lincoln’s skull (and the attached hair), as well as Gen. Daniel Sickles’ amputated leg and the unusual skull of a Civil War soldier who was shot across the top of the head. Other displays include small skeletons showcasing the different stages of a child’s development, a conjoined twin preserved in alcohol, and the mummified head and shoulders of a girl from the late 19th century. The museum is also home to one of the world’s largest neuroanatomical collections, consisting of normal and pathological human brains and comparative mammalian brains.

2. The Sourtoe Cocktail - Dawson City, Yukon

Many moons ago, miner and rumrunner Louie Linken had his frostbitten toe amputated and preserved in a jar of alcohol ... for posterity. Decades later, it was discovered by a local Yukon captain, who brought it to a saloon (now the Downtown Hotel bar) and started plopping it into folks’ drinks as a surprise garnish. The original toe lasted seven years before a replacement was needed, and since then, a whole foot’s worth of toes have been donated to the bar. For those who dream of joining the Sourtoe Cocktail Club, there’s only one rule: “You can drink it fast, you can drink it slow, but the lips have gotta touch the toe.”

3. Lindow Man - London, England

Scientists believe that this 25-year-old man died somewhere between 2 B.C. to A.D. 119. The bog he was found in left him remarkably well preserved, allowing for close study of his skin, hair, and internal organs. (The last meal in his stomach? Unleavened bread made from wheat and barley.) Examination of the man also revealed that his death was quite brutal, with head indentations, broken ribs, and a slashed throat indicating a prolonged struggle. It’s unclear whether his death was cold-blooded murder or part of a ritual sacrifice; either way, he clearly drew the short straw. Today, you can visit him at the British Museum to investigate his untimely demise yourself.

4. Preserved Head of Diogo Alves - Lisbon, Portugal

The head of Portugal’s first serial killer and one of its last men to ever be hanged now bobbles in a jar, passed by the unfazed medical students and professors of the University of Lisbon. When Alves met his demise in 1841, phrenology was an exciting, up-and-coming field, and Portugal’s eager phrenologists pleaded for his head to be preserved for study. By examining his skull, they believed they could determine why he killed so prolifically and ruthlessly. Did this pan out? Not really. (By 1843, phrenology was formally labeled a pseudoscience.) However, it’s a unique addition to an otherwise standard anatomical theater, sitting right next to a diaphanized hand.

5. Mütter Museum - Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

This collection inside the College of Physicians has everything: 2,000 objects removed from people’s throats, conjoined twin skeletons, the remains of a 7-foot-6-inch man, and, most notably, slivers of Albert Einstein’s brain. Displayed across 46 microscope slides, these strands have been studied extensively over the years, with some scientists suggesting that Einstein’s brain architecture gave him the “combinatory play” of image he claimed was essential to his discoveries. Others look at it and see ... just regular old brain matter, in less-than-ideal condition after its multiple trips across the country.

6. St. Anthony’s Tongue - Padua, Italy

St. Anthony was a renowned speaker during his lifetime, traveling across France and Italy preaching the word of God. Thus, it’s fitting that the one nondecomposed part of his body (exhumed in 1263) was his tongue. The saint’s tongue and jaw are now housed at his namesake basilica in Padua, displayed in ornate gold reliquaries that allow him to keep spreading the Gospel, even in death. The building itself is also a marvel, combining Romanesque, Byzantine, and Gothic architectural styles and housing artwork by Giotto and Donatello.

7. Transi de René de Chalon - Bar-le-Duc, France

Before Prince René de Chalon passed away at the age of 25, he specified that he did not want his dead body to look beautiful. Au contraire: René wanted to be remembered as a rotting corpse, with dried skin flaps and a hollow carcass. His wishes were granted in this grotesque, white-stone statue inside the Church of Saint-Étienne-le-Vieux, created by Ligier Richier in 1547. The heart-shaped reliquary in the statue’s hand once held the shriveled remains of René’s own heart; however, the heart was lost (or stolen...) during the French Revolution. Nevertheless, the ghoulish artwork is a dark reminder that all of us will go from “dust to dust.”

8. Chopin’s Heart - Warsaw, Poland

Composer Frédéric Chopin’s dying wish was that his heart be sent back to his native Poland rather than buried with the rest of his body in his adopted home of Paris. And what is family for if not to deliver on such requests? Chopin’s sister, Ludwika Jędrzejewicz, plucked out his heart before his interment, then smuggled it to Warsaw in a jar of booze. Placed beneath the city’s Holy Cross Church, the heart became a point of pride for Polish nationalists, so much so that the Nazis took it during World War II to weaken the country’s morale. (Thankfully, Germany returned it after the war.)

9. St. Valentine’s Shoulder Blade - Prague, Czechia

The shoulder bone of St. Valentine was supposedly brought to the Saints Peter and Paul Basilica in the 1300s by Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV, though it was not discovered until 2002, when church members found it while organizing the basement. Ever since, the shoulder blade has been on permanent display, with a special Mass honoring it on Valentine’s Day. Since many churches have claimed parts of St. Valentine over the years, there is some doubt about the authenticity of the bone. Whether this decorated shoulder belonged to the real saint or an imposter will likely remain a mystery forever, but regardless, it’s a wonderfully weird symbol of love.

10. Museum of Sin - Tambov, Russia

Forensic pathologist Yuri Shchukin has put his decades of morgue experience into this passion project: over 700 body parts and organs showing the ruinous effects of vice. Within his collection you’ll find such novelties as embryos from drinking and drug-taking mothers, the severed finger of an unfaithful husband, and a horn that supposedly sprouted from the head of a robber. A Latin inscription at the entrance reads: “This is a place where the dead teach the living.”

11. Galileo’s Middle Finger - Florence, Italy

Almost a century after Galileo was laid to rest, an antiquarian and an anatomist removed his middle finger, along with two other fingers and a tooth (why, exactly, is anyone’s guess). The finger was soon handed over to Florence’s Laurentian Library and, eventually, the Museo Galileo, where it is still on display today in an egg-shaped glass case with a marble base. A commemorative inscription by astronomer Tommaso Perelli reads: “Spurn not the remains of the finger by which the right hand measured out paths of the sky, pointed to orbs never before seen by mortals.” In 2009, Galileo’s middle finger had a heartwarming reunion with his newly authenticated index finger, thumb, and tooth.

12. St. Catherine’s Severed Head - Siena, Italy

When Saint Catherine died in 1380, her hometown of Siena wanted to keep her body but knew that Rome wouldn’t give it over willingly. So, the Sienese got creative: cutting off her head, putting it in a paper bag, and sneaking it past the Roman guards (praying for Catherine’s protection all the while). Upon their safe arrival back in Siena, these smugglers placed the head inside an ornate reliquary in the Basilica of San Domenico, where it remains today. Catherine’s thumb, too, is on display at the basilica, though her foot is all the way in Venice.

13. Buddha Tooth Relic Temple & Museum - Singapore

This enormous complex in Singapore’s Chinatown was erected for a single reason: to display one of the Buddha’s chompers, supposedly recovered from a collapsed stupa in Myanmar in the 1980s. (Never mind that some experts have called the tooth “definitely not human.”) Whether you believe in the tooth’s authenticity or not, it’s worth a visit to the temple just to take in its surroundings: multiple floors of Buddha statues, dragon snakes guarding sacred relics, and a stunning front prayer hall.

14. Kingship and Sacrifice - Dublin, Ireland

This permanent exhibition inside the National Museum of Ireland is devoted to Iron and Bronze Age human sacrifices that were deposited in bogs along tribal boundaries, a.k.a. “bog bodies.” The collection includes the Cashel Man, the oldest fleshed bog body ever unearthed, as well as the Gallagh Man, who was strangled by a willow twig rope. Along with the bodies themselves, visitors can view Iron Age artifacts like horse trappings, weapons, utensils, boundary markers, and votive deposits of butter known as “bog butter.”

15. Grave of Captain Jones’ Leg - Washington, New Hampshire

Capt. Samuel Jones, a beloved tavern proprietor in rural New Hampshire, was doing construction work one day in 1804 when his leg got pinned between a building and a fence. The resulting injury was so bad that Jones had to have the leg amputated, but he did not despair. Instead, he decided to hold a funeral for his lost limb and bury it in the local cemetery, in part as a precaution against phantom limb pain. When Jones passed away years later, his body was interred elsewhere (theories range from Boston to Rhode Island to the Bronx), but his leg remains here, marked by a simple gravestone.

item.title: Atlas Obscura’s Guide to America’s Most Haunted Cemeteries
item.dc:creator: Holyn Thigpen
item.description:
It’s nice to imagine death as an endless deep sleep, but not everyone is so lucky. In cemeteries across the U.S., you’ll find souls whose final resting places are not, in fact, restful at all. Perhaps they died with scores unsettled or, perhaps, their graves were ravaged by greedy developers. Sometimes, heartbreak rendered them unable to move on peacefully; in other cases, they simply couldn’t resist the chance to toy with their living visitors.

One thing is certain: These restless spirits can turn otherwise serene sites into delightfully dark destinations, where the beauty of old headstones and manicured grounds is tinged with something indescribably eerie. When you gear up for your next cross-country road trip, let the energy of spooky season guide you to these cemeteries and graveyards full of folklore, legend, and sinister rumors. They’re slices of history, yes, but they’re also brimming with all things supernatural, sure to turn even the most hardened paranormal skeptics into believers.

1. Colonial Park Cemetery - Savannah, Georgia

Established in 1750, this 6-acre site was Savannah’s primary public burial ground for over a century and contains over 9,000 graves. Many of the city’s earliest settlers are buried here, as well as hundreds of victims of the 1820 yellow fever epidemic. Some believe that when Savannah was overrun by Union forces during the Civil War, occupying soldiers dug up and moved around many of the cemetery’s headstones, also changing the names and dates etched into some of them. Understandably, this ruffled the feathers of the resident spirits, who now float through the cemetery as clouds of light or, sometimes, a green mist just above the ground.

Today, Colonial Park Cemetery is a public park, with haunted tours offered by various companies. While no visitors are permitted to the cemetery at night, some folks sit on benches just outside its fence to watch for apparitions. Some of Savannah’s ghost experts even conduct nighttime EVP (Electronic Voice Phenomenon) sessions just outside the cemetery walls, letting visitors listen to the strange sounds of thousands of spirits.

2. Harvard Shaker Lollipop Graveyard - Harvard, Massachusetts

This graveyard is weirdly whimsical thanks to its candy-esque cast-iron stakes, which mark the graves of many Shaker Village residents from decades past. The Shakers, a Christian religious collective with tenets of sexual equality, celibacy, and pacifism, settled this area in 1769, turning it into a self-contained society that lasted through the early 20th century.

The town is now a quiet historic district, though this does not mean that its residents have abandoned it; rather, locals have spotted deceased Shakers throughout the cemetery and in the surrounding fields and forests. It is also rumored that the graveyard was built upon a Native American burial ground, causing permanent unrest amongst the original inhabitants.

3. Dean Hill Cemetery - Fitchburg, Massachusetts

Also known as “The Rev,” this one-acre cemetery was established in 1791 as a burial site for Revolutionary War veterans and their families. Tucked away at the end of a secluded backroad, the cemetery is surrounded by worn stone walls, with many of the gravestones so weathered that it’s difficult to read the names on them. However, the people buried here still make themselves known ... over the years, locals have claimed to hear screams and see shadowy figures of Revolutionary War soldiers, as well as a mysterious woman dressed in all white. Legend even has it that, in the late ’80s or early ’90s, a ritual performed here opened a portal between worlds, though who orchestrated such a feat remains unknown.

4. Wildwood Cemetery and Crematorium - Williamsport, Pennsylvania

This cemetery has a unique design: It is split down the middle by a road that supposedly separates the eastern “good” side of the cemetery from the western “haunted” side, where the graves are older and the spirits are more restless. (It’s even rumored to house a banshee, who howls and sings sad songs in the night.) One of Wildwood’s mausoleums has some haunted history behind it, too. As the story goes, a local fireman was terrified of being buried alive and thus designed his mausoleum so that he could open it from inside. Nowadays, you can sometimes hear him moving around, waiting for a chance to stretch his legs on the cemetery grounds.

Wildwood is not only a prime place to interact with the dead but a wonderful place to be at one with nature. In fact, the cemetery was incorporated in 1863 because of the beauty and tranquility of its hilly landscape and then named Wildwood because of its thick woods. Don’t be surprised if you encounter a deer or two while exploring its haunted headstones or spot sparrows and hawks nestled in the trees.

5. Frenier Cemetery - LaPlace, Louisiana

About a 30-minute drive outside of New Orleans are the Manchac Wetlands, once home to the thriving towns of Ruddock, Napton, and Frenier. However, in 1915, a hurricane struck the area and destroyed all three, leaving many dead bodies in its wake. At least 29 of the hurricane’s victims were laid to rest in a mass grave inside Frenier Cemetery, but one woman, Julia Brown, was buried 100 yards away from the others. Why?

Brown was a rumored voodoo priestess, and Frenier residents alleged she said she would take the village with her when she died. The day the hurricane hit was the very same day she finally passed ... coincidence or voodoo magic, no one could say. Today, Brown is said to wander past the graves of those who perished in the storm, appearing to nearby kayakers behind layers of fog.

6. Georgiana Cemetery - Merritt Island, Florida

Moss-covered live oaks sway in the coastal breeze at this small Florida cemetery just off Merritt Island’s scenic South Tropical Trail. It’s a charming and relaxing spot ... that is, until you learn its history. It was here that, in 1934, 19-year-old Ethel Allen was buried after she was found brutally murdered on the banks of the Indian River Lagoon.

Perhaps because her murder was never solved (and justice was never served to her killer) Ethel still haunts Georgiana Cemetery, with many of its strange sights and sounds attributed to her. However, it seems as though Ethel may split her time between her burial site and the spot she was last seen alive, Ashley’s Tavern, where customers and employees have reported strange activity over the years.

7. Old Tonopah Cemetery - Tonopah, Nevada

If a cemetery is next to a Clown Motel, it’s probably safe to assume it’s haunted. Case in point is this relic of Tonopah’s silver days, where many former miners and prospectors are now buried. For the decade it was an active cemetery, from 1901 to 1911, over 300 people were interred here, many of them victims of the 1902 “Tonopah Plague” or the infamous Tonopah-Belmont Mine Fire of 1911. With such gruesome deaths, it makes sense that many of the cemetery’s residents would be on edge, seeking a respite from their underground abodes.

At the Clown Motel, EVPs have captured voices stating, “We mined” and “We died that day, 17 men” (in the mine fire), and guests have reported seeing eerie figures in the night, wandering through the halls or outside between the motel and the gravestones. Whether you hedge your bets and stay for the night or hightail it out of Tonopah before a ghost can grab you, the cemetery is sure to leave you sensing strange energy for days to come.

8. Alice Flagg’s Grave - Pawleys Island, South Carolina

In All Saints Cemetery, the ghost of Alice Flagg, a young woman who died shortly after being forcibly separated from her beloved, lingers just beside her grave. The plain marble slab bears only her first name, but visitors frequently adorn the spot with flowers and other small tokens of remembrance to help ease her heartbreak in the afterlife. Some even come to make a wish: It’s said that if you walk around her gravestone six times counterclockwise, then six times clockwise, then place a token on the letter “A,” your wish will be granted. When Alice isn’t here at her final resting place, she’s supposedly going up and down the stairs at the Flagg family home or floating through the rows of headstones at All Saints.

9. Greenwood Cemetery - Spokane, Washington

The staircase at this cemetery has been dubbed the “thousand steps” because, so the local lore goes, people rarely make it to the top. Those who do miraculously climb all the way up will see the faces of the dead men, women, and children buried below or hear their screams and cries ringing out in perpetuity. Some have even reported feeling a light, cool sensation much like rain while looking down from the highest step.

Tempting as it may be to try your luck on these spooky stairs, they are now part of private property and walking up or down them is considered trespassing. However, you can still view them from below by strolling through Greenwood Cemetery, which is itself home to many oddities. Abandoned tunnels under the cemetery, built by railroad companies in the late 19th century, may or may not be haunted by the Chinese laborers who died making them. Rumor also has it that the tunnels house buried treasure, but overgrown vegetation has prevented anyone from finding it.

10. Dead Children’s Playground - Huntsville, Alabama

Right next to Huntsville’s Maple Hill Cemetery is an interesting site: a simple playground with a swing set and small jungle gym, surrounded on three sides by dense trees and limestone walls. Given its proximity to over 80,000 burial plots, it’s only natural that the site would be slightly (or very) haunted. Over the years, adults and kids have witness swings moving on their own, as well as floating orbs of light. These odd occurrences could, perhaps, be signs from the many children who died during Huntsville’s 1918 flu epidemic. (Some visitors have heard laughing and squealing, so presumably they’re having a good time.)

11. Unitarian Church Cemetery - Charleston, South Carolina

Built in 1772, this is the second oldest cemetery in Charleston, with plots and graves overrun by vines, grass, and shrubs in an intentionally wild “cemetery garden design.” The decision to leave the cemetery undisturbed arose from the Unitarian belief in the interconnectedness of all things, living and dead, with natural growth showing how the spirit continues on even after the body is interred. In this case, it seems the spirits are especially active, as unusual occurrences are commonplace in the cemetery.

The identity of the cemetery’s ghostly “Lady in White” has long been subject to speculation, the most popular theory being that she is Annabel Lee, the subject of an 1849 Edgar Allan Poe poem inspired by local legend. In this story, Annabel, a young Charleston woman, carries on a clandestine affair with a sailor before dying of yellow fever. When the sailor is barred from attending her funeral, he keeps vigil for her in the spot they used to meet at night: the Unitarian Church Cemetery. Even if you don’t see poor Annabel, you may spot the cemetery’s other famous ghost, Mary Bloomfield. After her husband left for Boston and never returned, Mary spent the rest of her life heartbroken, and now, in death, she still searches for him amongst the graves.

12. St. Omer Cemetery Witch Grave - Ashmore, Illinois

This uniquely shaped gravestone belongs to Caroline Barnes, a young woman who was supposedly executed for magical crimes in the late 19th century. The impossible death date on her grave (February 31, 1882) is seen as proof of her supernatural powers, while the ball atop the grave is believed to be a crystal ball that lights up on the darkest nights. Also, those who’ve tried taking photos of the Barnes family plot say that their film won’t develop (however, pro tip: digital seems to do just fine). No matter the truth of this eerie tale, it has undoubtedly inspired some odd behavior at St. Omer, namely, nighttime rituals that have left the site covered in flowers, coins, and candles.

13. El Campo Santo Cemetery - San Diego, California

Translating to “Holy Field” Cemetery, this small grave site in Old Town San Diego is the last remaining part of what was once a much larger cemetery. As the city grew rapidly in the late 19th century, parts of the grounds were paved over to accommodate streetcars (feeding a theory that the spirits of El Campo are now trapped beneath the concrete). However, white crosses have been painted over parts of the surrounding street and sidewalks to honor some of these disrespected graves, while small brass markers denote others.

El Campo Santo is the resting place of several Native American leaders, including Antonio Garra, a mid-19th-century Kupa chief who was executed by a firing squad right next to his open grave. Now, he’s one of the cemetery’s most spotted specters, overpowering visitors with intense chills, feelings of sorrow, and faint whispers. The other most famous ghost here is Yankee Jim Robinson, a drifter convicted of grand larceny for trying to steal a rowboat. Jim was hanged just down the road from El Campo, and his spirit now wanders the grounds, begging for forgiveness.

item.title: It All Comes Together in Chattanooga
item.dc:creator: Daniel McDermon
item.description:
Chattanooga may be best known for its natural beauty, surrounded by mountains, valleys, and the Tennessee River. This charming Appalachian city is also home to annual music festivals like the IBMA World of Bluegrass and the 3 Sisters Bluegrass Festival. The streets and venues fill with musicians and fans dedicated to upholding the traditions of bluegrass music.

Chattanooga has always been a city of convergence. Long before trains arrived, the river drew people through a narrow passage in the mountains; later came traders, artists, and entrepreneurs. At festival time, bluegrass becomes the city's soundtrack, with impromptu performances and jams ranging all across town. Many of the local hot spots are pressed into service as music venues.

The destinations collected here allow for all sorts of gatherings: a railroad terminal built to serve historic crowds, now repurposed; a riverfront freighted with Cherokee history where folks now gather for performances; and even a whiskey company that rallied the community to change state law. Taken as a whole, they reveal a city profoundly shaped around the possibilities of people coming together.

Chattanooga Choo Choo — Historic Terminal Station

Begin at the building that made Chattanooga synonymous with arrival. Terminal Station opened in 1909 and at its peak handled nearly 50 trains a day, turning its grand waiting room into a literal crossroads of travelers, soldiers, workers, and families. Passenger service ended in 1970, but the station survived demolition and was reborn as the Chattanooga Choo Choo. Today the former terminal is once again centered around travel: the Hotel Chalet, restaurants, music venues, comedy, gardens, and Station Street all radiate from the old rail hub.

The New Mountain Opry

On Walden’s Ridge atop Signal Mountain, neighbors, musicians, and visitors have been uniting around music for years, sharing both a room and a repertoire. The original Mountain Opry began in 1979 and spent more than four decades presenting bluegrass and folk music at the Walden’s Ridge Civic Center before being reborn at the historic Bachman Community Center in 2021 as the New Mountain Opry. It lives on as a monthly tradition, with live bluegrass in the old school auditorium.

Tennessee River Gorge

Follow the river west into the landscape that made Chattanooga a crossroads long before there was a city here. The Tennessee River Gorge runs for roughly 27 miles through the Cumberland Mountains, and archaeological evidence points to human presence here for at least 10,000 years. The river served as a travel corridor, and more recently communities, commerce, military movements, and industry have all depended on navigating through this narrow passage. Today the Tennessee River Gorge Trust protects more than 17,000 acres of the gorge and promotes hiking, paddling, camping, research, and education — turning an ancient corridor into a modern destination for conservation and outdoor life. Among other events, the gorge hosts Chattajack, a 31-mile paddleboard and kayak race. Visitors should also explore Williams Island, home to hundreds of acres of wilderness and only accessible by boat.

Ross’s Landing

Ross’s Landing, along the riverfront, was associated with Cherokee businessman and later Principal Chief John Ross, serving as a ferry and trading location. In 1838, it also became a departure point during the forced removal of Cherokee people on the Trail of Tears. An art installation in the park commemorates their forcible departure. Today the riverfront is once again a major public space, with lawns, an amphitheater, a marina, promenades, and interpretive features hosting local events like Riverfront Nights free summer concert series and the Chattanooga River Games. Just upstream, the Walnut Street bridge reopened in October 2026, restoring one of downtown’s best-loved pedestrian connections across the Tennessee River after a major renovation.

The Read House Hotel

Classic hospitality can be found here, at Chattanooga’s oldest hotel. The Read House traces its hotel history back roughly 150 years, while its present interiors lean into the glamour of the 1920s. Its most famous story belongs to Room 311: The room is said to be haunted by the ghost of Annalisa Netherly, a guest from the 1920s. Tours keep the tale alive. The grand lobby and lively barroom conversation make this a hot spot for visitors to share their stories.

Chattanooga Whiskey Experimental Distillery

At Chattanooga Whiskey, the convivial spirit turned into political action. When the company was founded in 2011, state law still prevented distilling spirits in Hamilton County. Its founders launched the “Vote Whiskey” campaign, held public events, and pushed for a change in Tennessee law. The change passed into law in 2013, making legal distilling possible in the city again for the first time in more than a century. Production began at the Experimental Distillery in 2015, and regular tours are available, along with tastings of their signature Tennessee High Malt whiskey.

Bluff View Art District

Set above the Tennessee River in a historic downtown district, Bluff View brings together the River Gallery, sculpture garden, Bluff View Inn, Rembrandt’s Coffee House, Tony’s Pasta Shop, a bakery, patios, paths, and scenic overlooks. The appeal is less a single attraction than the way all of the pieces connect: art leads to coffee, coffee to a garden, and the garden to a view across the river.

Chickamauga Battlefield

In September 1863, Union and Confederate armies collided at Chickamauga in one of the Civil War’s bloodiest battles; the battlefield later became part of the nation’s first national military park. Over time, a second layer of communal memory accumulated here: ghost stories, especially the local legend of “Old Green Eyes.” There are many explanations for this mysterious apparition. One suggests it’s the spirit of a soldier. Another says the ghostly presence was there long before the Civil War. An annual October festival celebrates the legend. It’s just another example of how history and myth can exist in the same remarkable landscape.

item.title: The Best Haunted Hotels to Book for a Spooky Getaway
item.dc:creator: Holyn Thigpen
item.description:
Nothing beats staying in a hotel whose suites hold some stories — especially if they’re of the spooky variety. The same friends who roll their eyes at mentions of luxury amenities and amazing views will be wide-eyed when you tell them about the ghost you accidentally ate breakfast with, the wailings you heard on your way to the icebox, or your run-in with an uncanny Victorian woman wearing all black. Booking a room at a regular old hotel will give you a few nice photos and a comfy robe; booking a room at a haunted one will give you tales of terror to tell for the rest of your life.

At these hotels, lodges, inns, and resorts around the world, the supernatural is embraced and the unsettling is celebrated. Unexplained occurrences are simply part of the experience, and those with a healthy level of morbid curiosity will find no shortage of places to explore. Here, dark lore is hidden in every nook and cranny: a quack doctor’s treatment room, geothermal soaking pools, an old-school saloon, and a clown statue collection. Look over your shoulder and you might spot a glowing orb, a sopping-wet child, or a murderous outlaw. No matter where on this list you choose to book your stay, get ready to expect the unexpected.

Prices shown are approximate starting rates for a standard double room per night, based on rates current as of September 2026. Rates vary significantly by season — expect higher prices in October. USD figures for non-US properties are approximate conversions.

Hotel From / night Ghost Tours Notes

St. James Hotel Cimarron, New Mexico, USA ~$115 On request No A/C or TVs in historic rooms. Annex rooms have modern amenities. Book direct: (575) 376-2664. exstjames.com
